## The rubric lane has data in it, and doctrine beats baseline on test quality

The lane built in Phase 14 and never written to by any epoch now holds **9 records**,
reviewer `model-judge qwen3.8-27b (blind paired, order-swapped, n=3 per order)`. Full
report: [quality-epoch14.md](quality-epoch14.md).

### The judge earned the right to be believed first

Calibration ran twice, on separate invocations, and returned **6/6 both times** with
every identical-pair control clean. It separated a suite asserting nothing from a real
one, a suite that recomputes the implementation's own regex from one naming literal
outputs, dead scaffold, a strategy registry for a one-function task, and a dropped edge
case. **Three of those six cases have the SHORTER tree as the better one**, so a judge
preferring more code scores 50%; this one scored 100%.

That answers the question the handoff left open — a local 27B can judge this — and the
answer is not an assumption anywhere below.

### The result

| arm | cells | structure | decomposition | **testQuality** | deadCode | overBuilding |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 4 | 3 | 3 | **1** | 2 | 3 |
| doctrine | 4 | 3 | 3 | **3** | 2 | 2 |
| conductor | 1 | 0 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 3 |

The paired verdicts agree with the medians, which is the check that matters: on
`testQuality`, **doctrine beat baseline on 3 of 4 tasks and tied the fourth, losing
none** — each win unanimous across both presentation orders and three seeds.

**This is the first evidence in fourteen epochs that any arm produces better-considered
work than one model turn, and it belongs to doctrine — the arm with no plugin, no state
machine and no sub-sessions.** Doctrine costs 3.4-7.4x baseline wall clock for it.

The conductor row is one cell on the corpus's cheapest task, where it changed 1,342
bytes. It won no criterion against anyone. Against doctrine it lost `structure` and
`decomposition`; its `testQuality` never resolved. **The arm the campaign exists to
justify remains unmeasured on the axis that would justify it**, because it produced
nothing to measure on three of four tasks.

### What the run could not resolve, and why it is the instrument's fault

**16 of 30 real comparisons returned `no_verdict`**, almost all of them
`the judge spent its whole token budget reasoning and never answered`. One
(`doctrine vs conductor` on `testQuality`) was 6 of 6 unusable.

The cause is a calibration corpus that is **not representative of the workload in the
one dimension that mattered**. Its fixtures are ~1k-token prompts; the real trees render
3-12k. The judge passed calibration and then ran out of budget on the actual job, which
is a calibration that certified the wrong thing. `--max-tokens 3000` was itself the fix
for a 700-token budget that produced zero usable answers; the number moved and the
failure mode did not.

The rule this earns: **a calibration corpus has to match the real inputs in size, not
only in kind.** Sizing cases by what is convenient to write is how a passing calibration
stops predicting anything.

Three cells were correctly refused a rubric record — `conductor/clock-inject-py`,
`conductor/euler-cli-py`, `conductor/logfmt-lenses-ts` — reported as
`a gap, not a zero` rather than scored 0, which would have read as a quality judgement
about work that does not exist.

### Incidental: the throughput prediction held

The judging ran at `--concurrency 3`, achieving **mean slot concurrency 2.87 over 2,000
samples**, against **1.06** measured across epoch 14. Calibration alone took 31 minutes
where the measured serial call latency implies 73 — a **2.34x speedup**, inside the
2-2.5x that
[the throughput plan](../../plans/2026-08-25-throughput-and-serving-parameters.md)
predicted from bandwidth arithmetic. Item 3 of that plan is done and its prediction is
no longer arithmetic.

## What `bench/conductor-tasks.json` can and cannot answer

The crawl-before-walk handoff opens by saying the campaign measured the wrong manifest,
because *"`bench/conductor-tasks.json`'s prompts contain the decomposition"*, and cites
`tetris-py` — four modules, twelve signatures, the dependency order and the scoring table
handed over in a numbered list.

That citation is accurate and `tetris-py` is quoted correctly. **It is also a task no epoch
ever ran.** Before recording the premise, it was checked against the manifest and against
epoch 14's own result files.

### The handover, measured across all 23 tasks

Counting, per prompt, the numbered list items and the distinct `src/…` module paths it
names:

| tasks | numbered plan | module paths named | reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| `textkit-cpp`, `euler-suite-py`, `snake-game-ts`, `tetris-py` | 4 items each | 0–8 | the decomposition is handed over |
| `logfmt-lenses-ts`, `euler-solvers-py` | none | 5–8 | the file split is handed over as prose |
| the other 17 | none | 0–2 | one or two seams pinned, nothing more |

So the manifest is not uniformly plan-bearing. Six of 23 tasks hand over a file split; the
other seventeen pin a seam, which is the shape the handoff credits only to
`bench/corpus-euler.json`.

### Epoch 14 ran four tasks, and three of them hand over nothing

`.data/benchmark/watch/20260825-172722` holds 20 cells over exactly four task ids —
`slugify-ts` (T0), `euler-cli-py` (T1), `logfmt-lenses-ts` (T2), `clock-inject-py` (T4).
None of the four numbered-plan tasks is among them.

- `slugify-ts` — one function in one file. Behaviour stated, no plan, nothing to decompose.
- `euler-cli-py` — pins `src/cli.py` exporting `main(argv)` and lists five behaviours
  observable through it. **This is a seam-pinned prompt**, structurally the same shape as
  the euler corpus the handoff proposes as the replacement.
- `clock-inject-py` — pins three names and two constraints (*"do not change any function
  signature, and do not thread a clock argument through the callers"*). The design that
  satisfies them is left entirely open.
- `logfmt-lenses-ts` — **the one that does hand it over.** *"Add four more, each in its own
  file"*, then names all four files and specifies each one's output format.

**The premise as written is false for the set that was actually measured.** Three of the
four prompts hand over no plan.

### The conclusion survives, by a different route

What all four measured tasks share is not a handed-over plan. It is that **none of them
requires a multi-part decomposition to be invented.** Three have nothing to decompose;
the fourth has its decomposition dictated. The campaign has therefore never put a
decomposition in front of any arm — which is the handoff's bottom line, reached from the
evidence rather than from `tetris-py`.

This matters for the ladder. `bench/corpus-euler.json` is a legitimate **crawl** rung, but
against `euler-cli-py` it is a *lateral* move in decomposition terms, not a step down: both
pin one seam and leave the interior open. Its value is that it asks the same question
twenty times with a verified answer behind it, against an arm that went **0 for 4** in
epoch 14. It is not a first measurement of decomposition and the manifest's own
`selectionCriteria` says so — *"one Euler problem is one solver module plus one import line
however hard the mathematics is."*

### What the old manifest still supports

- **Cost ratios.** Doctrine at 3.4–7.4x baseline wall clock, conductor at its ceiling on
  3 of 4 tasks. Unaffected by what the prompt hands over.
- **The `testQuality` result**, and it arguably strengthens. Doctrine beat baseline on 3 of
  4 tasks and tied the fourth — and on `slugify-ts`, `euler-cli-py` and `clock-inject-py`
  the plan was *not* handed over, so that win is not an artifact of a dictated file split.
- **The conductor arm's failure to produce anything.** 3 timeouts and 1 fail out of 4, on
  tasks whose prompts ask for one or two files.

### What it cannot support

Any claim about planning or decomposition, in either direction — because no arm was ever
asked for one. That is a gap in the task set, not a result about the harness, and the
`logfmt-lenses-ts` cells cannot be repaired into one: their file split is in the prompt.

## D44 — the campaign runs a router binary six days older than its own ledger writer

`faf4458` ("the ledger says when", 2026-08-26 17:42) added `completedAt` to every router
ledger line. Its acceptance was `ctest` green. Two hours later, every ledger line the
step-1 run produced looked like this:

```
{"completionTokens":289,"group":null,"model":"qwen3.8-27b","priority":"interactive",
 "promptTokens":11724,"queueWaitMs":0,"role":null,"schemaConformed":null,
 "schemaMissing":null,"status":200,"timings":{…},"upstreamMs":20714}
```

No `completedAt`. The field is in `router/metrics.hpp:251` and is absent from the wire.

### The cause, reproduced rather than inferred

```
$ ls -la .out/build/clang-relwdebinfo/llama-router
-rwxr-xr-x  3007936  Aug 20 16:14  .out/build/clang-relwdebinfo/llama-router

$ git log --since="2026-08-20 16:14" --oneline -- router/
faf4458 instruments: the server publishes its own counters and the ledger says when
bcc528e Rename to llama-leash and drop the absorbed corpus repo's references
c750d9a conductor: 13.2 live smoke
e5b0ad9 repo cleanup: drop completed-campaign scaffolding, repair stale references
```

The binary in the campaign's search path predates four commits to `router/`. Nothing in
`scripts/conductor_wiring.py` rebuilds it — `find_router_binary` takes the first
executable it finds over a pinned relpath list and asks nothing about its age.

**`ctest` structurally cannot catch this.** `CMakeLists.txt` builds `llama-router` from
`router/main.cpp` and `router-tests` from `router/tests/*.cpp`. They are two targets;
building the second does not relink the first. The suite compiles the header the campaign
never loads.

### Why it is worse than one missing field

This is D42's shape — *"a stale bytecode cache hid the fix"* — recurring one layer down,
and the register already names that class. What is specific here is the blast radius: the
router ledger is the campaign's **only** per-request instrument. It carries
`promptTokens`, `completionTokens`, `upstreamMs`, `queueWaitMs` and the decode timings
that every cost claim in this document rests on. A stale router does not fail loudly; it
serves requests correctly and writes an older schema, so the measurement degrades
silently and the campaign reads exactly the same.

It also blocks R11 from the euler-001 forensics — *"join the router ledger to the journal"*
— which needs `completedAt` to align a ledger row with the journal `inject` that caused
it. The join was recorded as available; it is not.

### The fix

`conductor_wiring.router_sources_newer_than(binary, root)` returns the `router/*.hpp` and
`router/*.cpp` files modified after the binary was linked, excluding `router/tests/`
because those link into the other target. `router_staleness_refusal` renders the operator
message, and `run_and_watch.preflight` **refuses the run** rather than warning:

```
  router binary STALE
                llama-router at .out/build/clang-relwdebinfo/llama-router was built
                before 1 of its own source file(s):
                  router/metrics.hpp
                The ledger a run is scored on is written by the binary, not by the
                tree, so a run started here measures the older router and says
                nothing about the change. Rebuild it with:
                  cmake --build .out/build/clang-relwdebinfo --target llama-router
```

Refusing costs one rebuild. Not refusing costs a campaign measured on an instrument
nobody checked.

**Guarded by** six cases in `scripts/test_conductor_wiring.py::RouterBinaryFreshness`,
including the two that keep the check honest: `router/tests/*.cpp` newer than the binary
must **not** trip it, and a *missing* binary must not be reported as stale — absent and
out-of-date are different findings with different remedies, and `find_router_binary`
already owns the first.

The check was then run against the real tree and named `router/metrics.hpp` and nothing
else, which is the file `faf4458` touched. That is the reproduction, not the hypothesis.

### The standing question this leaves

The step-1 cells were already in flight when this was found, so **their ledger rows have
no `completedAt`**. Nothing in step 1's reading depends on it — decode rate and completion
volume come from `timings` and `upstreamMs`, both present — but the crawl-rung campaign
must not start until the rebuild has happened.

## The gate's live leg and a campaign cell cannot share the machine

Running `bash scripts/test-conductor.sh` while a conductor cell was executing produced:

```
TAP: tests=2056 pass=2048 fail=1 cancelled=7
not ok 852 - live injection through a real opencode (GAP-003)
  failureType: 'hookFailed'
  error: 'opencode serve /config never became ready: TimeoutError'
  duration_ms: 44673.7
```

One hook failure, seven cancelled children. `conductor/tests/live-inject.test.ts` boots its
**own** `opencode serve` and waits for `/config`; the conductor arm was running an
orchestrator plus a classifier sub-session against the same 27B, and the new server never
got scheduled inside its timeout.

**It is contention, not a regression, and the decisive evidence is not the error text.**
The working tree at that moment held six modified files — `arm_report.py`,
`conductor_wiring.py`, `run_and_watch.py`, two test modules and this document. **No
TypeScript.** `live-inject.test.ts` exercises the opencode plugin, so no edit in that set
can reach it. An earlier run of the same gate, at HEAD, printed `GATE PASS` — while the
*doctrine* cell was live, which is one opencode process rather than three.

Two things follow, and the second is the one worth keeping.

**Operationally:** the gate is not safe to run against a live campaign. Its acceptance
reading has to be taken on a quiet machine, or the run has to be paused for it.

**On the suite's design:** this surfaced as a *failure* only because
`gap-003-noskip` asserts the live leg actually ran —

> opencode is installed, so the live leg MUST have run: a leg that silently stops driving
> the real binary is indistinguishable from one that passes

Without that case the timeout would have degraded into a skip, the gate would have printed
a green over a leg that never drove the binary, and the campaign would have been the third
thing in this register to be certified by a measurement of nothing. It is the same rule the
`seedDir` and `completedAt` findings above turn on: **the failure mode to guard is not a
wrong answer, it is a well-formed empty one.**

---

## A cell loads the plugin from the working tree, so an edit during a run rewrites the experiment

Every conductor cell's generated `conductor.json` names the plugin by absolute path into
the checkout being worked in:

```json
"plugin": ["/Users/sal/development/vorlac/llama-harness/conductor/plugin/index.ts"]
```

Not a copy, not a pinned revision — the live tree. A cell that starts at 19:58 and ends at
20:43 is running whatever `conductor/` says during those forty-five minutes.

For a four-cell epoch watched by a person this is invisible and harmless. For the
twenty-task crawl rung it is not: sixty cells over roughly a day is long enough that the
temptation to fix something mid-run is the normal case rather than the exception, and a
fix landing at cell 31 splits the campaign into two experiments reported as one. Nothing
in the run records which revision a cell actually loaded, so the split would not be
visible afterwards either.

This is D44's shape a third time — **the artifact measured is not the artifact named.**
D44 was a binary older than its source; the `seedDir` finding was a report reading the
wrong dialect; this is a source tree that can move underneath a run in progress.

**Working rule for the crawl rung, adopted now:** no edit to `conductor/`, `bench/` or
`scripts/` while cells are in flight. The step-1 fix for D10 below waits for its own cell
to finish for exactly this reason, even though the fix is known and the cell is failing on
the defect it repairs.

The durable version — stamping each cell's result with the `git rev-parse HEAD` and dirty
state of the tree it loaded — is not built here and is recorded as the thing that would
make the rule checkable rather than remembered.

# Step 1 of the crawl rung — `euler-001-py`, three arms at HEAD, 2026-08-26

The crawl-before-walk handoff asks for one thing before twenty cells inherit anything:
reproduce `euler-001-py` three-arm at HEAD, because the two prior runs of that cell both
predate the stalled-turn detector, the inline-claim refusal, the derived mechanics and the
per-role deadlines. All four are confirmed present in this tree.

## The result

| arm | outcome | wall | prompt tok | completion tok | produced |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| baseline | **pass** | 4.4 min | 99,608 | 3,335 | a working solver |
| doctrine | **pass** | 9.4 min | 239,757 | 5,939 | a working solver |
| conductor | **timeout** | 45.0 min | 340,006 | 27,636 | **nothing** |

The conductor tree at the ceiling is byte-for-byte the seed. The gauge ran and failed
exit 1 because `p001` does not exist — a cleaner accounting than 2026-08-21, where a
timeout skipped the gauge and the report read `0/0`.

**Doctrine costs 2.12x baseline wall clock here, against 4.7x on 2026-08-21.** The served
window is now 3 slots x 65,536 rather than 6 x 32,768, so opencode's compaction threshold
(`context - min(20000, output)`) sits at ~57k instead of 24,576. The doctrine arm crossed
the old threshold three times in the forensics run and crosses the new one never. That is
the single largest improvement visible in this cell, and it belongs to a serving flag
rather than to the harness.

## Third loss, third distinct cause — and they must not be merged

The handoff is explicit that the two prior losses had different causes and must not be
conflated. This one is a third, and it is neither of them.

| # | date | reached | cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-08-21 | never left INTAKE | cluster-extractor defect (fixed in `planning.ts`) |
| 2 | 2026-08-21 | EXECUTING, zero bytes | the G8/§2.4 fork (R1/R2 landed) |
| 3 | **2026-08-26** | **DECOMPOSED, zero bytes** | **D10 flipped the classification, and the work route does not fit T1** |

Neither of the two fixed causes recurred. The run got past both and lost to something else.

## The timeline, from the journal's own clock

```
 0.0 –  1.7 min   startup
 1.7 –  7.9 min   classify attempt 1: three tries, all "response was not parseable JSON"  ← D10
 7.9 min          conductor_classify refused
 8.9 min          conductor_decompose refused from INTAKE                                 ← D11
 9.0 – 11.0 min   classify re-waved → "work"
11.0 – 15.8 min   skeptic agrees "work"
15.8 min          FSM → INTAKE
16.2 – 24.6 min   planner decomposes → 2 items
24.6 min          FSM → DECOMPOSED
25.1 – 45.0 min   conductor_plan: one planner sub-session, still generating at the ceiling
45.0 min          wall clock expires
```

24 injected requests in 2,700 s — **112.5 s per model call, 1,152 completion tokens per
call.** Every number below is derived from those two.

## D10 at n=3, and the consequence the register does not yet record

The discarded reply was 1,346 characters and ended:

```
..."ladderRung":"minimal-code"}}
```

Programmatically checked rather than eyeballed: it does **not** end inside a string, and
its unclosed-delimiter stack is exactly `['{']`. **Short by one `}`**, the same shape as
epoch 3's 1,565-character reply ending `..."ladderRung":"one-liner"}}`.

D10 is recorded as costing about ten minutes. Here it cost 7.3 minutes of retries and
refusals — and something the register does not have:

> **The discarded reply said `trivial`. The re-roll said `work`.**

The thrown-away object was complete and correct — `kind: trivial`, `fileScope`
`["src/solvers/p001.py", "src/solvers/__init__.py"]`, `testScope`
`["tests/check_visible.py"]`. Balancing its one brace parses it and recovers all of it.

**A claim made here on first reading, and withdrawn by the post-fix re-run: that D10 is
what selected the branch.** It is not. The re-run recovered a `trivial` verdict intact,
the skeptic agreed with it, and the run landed on `work` anyway — escalated by the §3.2
acceptance-cluster budget, which neither D10 nor the skeptic can reach. D10's cost is the
retries and the minutes. The branch is decided downstream, and by something else; see
*the classifier is judged by a rule it is never shown* below.

## The T1 budget question, answered with this cell's own numbers

At the measured 112.5 s per model call, **T1 (2,700 s) buys 24 model calls.** The demand,
counting a sequential-equivalent call per orchestrator turn and per sub-session:

| route | minimum model calls | seconds | share of T1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| trivial, 1 item | 16 | 1,800 | **67%** |
| work, 2 items | ~47 | ~5,290 | **196%** |

The trivial figure is 9 orchestrator turns (classify, inline_claim, submit_test, vet_test,
mark_green, validate, item_review, publish, report — the stage order is
`conductor/doctrine/core.md:108`) plus 7 sub-sessions (classifier, skeptic, testWriter,
1 vet critic under `TRIVIAL_VET_CRITICS`, 3 item-review lenses under the trivial
composition). Only the 3 lenses can overlap, so perfect wave parallelism buys 14 rather
than 16 — about 12%.

The work figure adds a decompose planner, a plan planner, 4 plan reviewers, and then runs
the six-stage item pipeline **twice**, at `itemReviewers 6` and `vetCritics 3` rather than
the trivial 3 and 1.

So the answers the handoff asked for:

**Is the T1 mismatch real?** Yes, and it is worse than a mismatch on the work route — it
is a factor of two. On the trivial route T1 fits with a third to spare.

**Is it a fan-out problem?** No. 13 of the trivial route's 16 calls are strictly serial:
the 9 orchestrator turns are a state machine, and classify's classifier→skeptic pair is a
data dependency. Cutting fan-out cannot close a gap that fan-out did not open. This also
means the unresolved contradiction between the forensics' 1.09x concurrency figure and the
quality judge's 2.34x is **not load-bearing here**, and no probe was built to settle it.

**What binds, then?** Which route the classifier picks. That is a one-word verdict that
decides a 3x difference in demand, and in this run it was decided by a missing brace.

## What the run did well, which is the part worth not losing

The planner's decomposition is good. Two items, correct dependency
(`p001_registration` dependsOn `p001_solver`), disjoint `fileScope`s, and acceptance rows
that faithfully restate the prompt's anti-hardcode constraints — including the right
answer, 233168, where the classifier's own acceptance row had written 233163.

**This is the campaign's thesis demonstrated and defeated in the same cell.** The harness
can decompose this problem, and produced a better artifact doing it than its own classifier
did. It arrived at minute 24.6 of 45, with a two-item pipeline still ahead.

It also clears a hazard worth recording as cleared: both `testScope` paths the planner
chose — `tests/check_p001.py` and `tests/check_p001_registration.py` — match the euler
seed's `check_*.py` verify glob, so this corpus does **not** carry the
testScope-unreachable-by-itemTest defect that wedged two epoch-14 cells. That alignment is
luck rather than design: nothing tells the planner what the runner globs, and it
pattern-matched `tests/check_visible.py` out of the prompt.

## Two observations handed to D43 rather than acted on

D43 is reserved for its own session and nothing here starts it. Two facts this cell
produced belong to it:

- **The `conductor_plan` planner ran 19.9 minutes against a 20-minute `planner` role
  deadline** (`ROLE_TIMEOUT_MS`), so the deadline was about six seconds from firing when
  the cell ceiling fired instead. A deadline that never gets to act is not evidence the
  deadline is wrong, and this cell cannot distinguish the two.
- **Inside those 19.9 minutes is one 10.7-minute gap** (30.6 → 41.3) containing a single
  model turn and one `bash` call. Around it the planner ran `bash`, `glob` and eight
  `read`s — re-deriving a tree it had just been handed a 6,099-character decomposition of.

## Disclosure — this cell's wall clock is not clean

`bash scripts/test-conductor.sh` was run for about four minutes during this cell, which
booted a second `opencode serve` and 2,056 tests on the same machine. It does not change
the verdict — the cell was still writing its execution plan at minute 25 with a two-item
pipeline ahead of it, and four minutes does not buy 47 model calls — but the 45.0-minute
figure includes contention that a clean run would not have, and the 27,636 completion
tokens are correspondingly low against the 38,288 of 2026-08-21. Recorded rather than
quietly left in the table.

## D10 fixed — the repair is the one the register specified three epochs ago

Epoch 3 wrote the fix down and nobody built it:

> A deterministic repair before declaring the reply schema-invalid (balance the braces,
> re-parse, accept if it validates) would have cost microseconds.

`conductor/adapter/fanout.ts` now carries `closeUnterminated`, tried inside
`readJsonDocument` after the existing in-string control-character escape and before the
reply is declared unparseable. It appends closing delimiters and never content.

### What it refuses, which is the load-bearing half

Two shapes it could technically close and does not:

- a document that ends **inside a string**, and
- a document whose last meaningful character is **`,` or `:`**.

Both are a value cut mid-word rather than a document cut after one. Closing them would
manufacture a well-formed object out of a partial answer and hand it on as the model's
reply — worse than the retry it saves, because a retry is visible and a fabricated
completion is not. What survives the filter is the case where every value present is
complete and only the closers are absent.

It also cannot buy an acceptance. A repaired document still has to `JSON.parse` **and**
pass `validate`, so a balanced document of the wrong shape is refused exactly as an
unbalanced one was — pinned by its own case.

### Verified against the artifact, not against a reimplementation

The 1,346-character reply the crawl cell discarded was written out of the journal and fed
to the **shipped** `createFanout`, over a stub client that returns those exact bytes:

```
attempts        : 1
kind            : trivial
fileScope       : ["src/solvers/p001.py","src/solvers/__init__.py"]
testScope       : ["tests/check_visible.py"]
```

One attempt, no retry, and the verdict the run threw away is recovered whole. The
arithmetic had already been done in Python; running it again through the TypeScript that
actually ships is the point, because "the same algorithm" is precisely the reasoning D44
above shows to be unsafe.

### The nesting case is a discriminator, checked as one

`[D10] mixed nesting left open is closed innermost first` ends a reply with four
delimiters open in the order `{ [ { [`. Closed innermost-first the document parses and
then fails the probe schema; closed in any other order it does not parse at all:

```
innermost-first    PARSES
reversed           parse error: Expected ',' or ']' after array element
```

So the assertion — *the surviving complaint is the schema's, not the parser's* — separates
a correct stack from a reversed one. A case that only asked "did it fail" would pass
against a broken implementation, which is the trap this campaign has paid for repeatedly.

**Guarded by** five cases in `conductor/tests/fanout.test.ts`, three for the repair and two
for the refusals. Gate: `GATE PASS` (2,061 node tests, up from 2,056), `M5 PASS`, ctest
green.

### What this does and does not buy

It removes 7.3 minutes from the crawl cell and, more importantly, removes the mechanism
that flipped the classification onto a route that cannot fit T1. It does **not** make the
conductor arm pass `euler-001-py`. On the trivial route the process floor is still 67% of
T1, the classification's stability is still unmeasured at n=1 per verdict, and the
`conductor_plan` planner still spent 19.9 minutes re-reading a tree it had been handed.
Whether the arm completes the cell is a question for the re-run, not for this section.

## D45 — the classifier is judged by a rule it is never shown

The post-fix re-run of `euler-001-py` (2026-08-26, `step2-euler001-postfix`) recovered the
`trivial` verdict D10 had been discarding, the skeptic **agreed** with it — and the run
landed on `work` regardless:

```
fsm guard-reject {"stage":"classify","disposition":"escalate-to-work","violations":[
  "item \"I1\" is too large: its acceptance spans 3 clusters
   (src/solvers/p001.py, register, get), over the one-cluster item budget (§3.2)"]}
```

### First, what this is NOT, because the register already argued it

`grep -ril cluster docs/build/artifacts/` before theorising — the rule this campaign wrote
for itself after D25. Doing so finds `acceptance-cluster-defect.md` (553 lines) and D25's
withdrawal:

> ~~The one-cluster budget is too strict~~ **WITHDRAWN: the guard is correct and
> documented; the planner is not writing subject-first criteria.**

That withdrawal is right and this is not a reopening. The guard's computation reproduces
byte-for-byte off a bare `node` import of `acceptanceClusters` against the item the run
actually produced:

```
REAL acceptance -> 3 cluster(s): ["src/solvers/p001.py","register","get"]

per-row contribution:
  0 ["src/solvers/p001.py"]   1 ["register"]   2 ["get"]
  3 ["solve"]                 4 ["solve"]      5 []   6 []

same criteria, subject fronted -> 1 cluster(s): ["src/solvers/p001.py"]
```

The rule is **satisfiable**, and an early guess that it might be structurally unreachable
for a registry task is refuted by the last line. Rows 3 and 4 yield `solve` alone and fold
into the file in the full list, because row 0 names the file and `solve` beside each other
— the documented homing property working exactly as written.

### What is new is which role is at fault

D25's withdrawal says the remedy is that the criterion-writer open each criterion with its
subject, *"which the generated mechanics block already instructs it to do."* That is true of
the planner and **false of the classifier.**

```
conductor/adapter/inject.ts:44
  planner:    ["decompose.md", "plan.md"]
  mechanical: ["core.md"]
```

`decompose.md:104` carries the instruction verbatim — *"open each criterion with what it is
about (`parse rejects empty input`, not `rejects empty input`)"*. `core.md` mentions neither
clusters nor criterion subjects; the count is zero. The `mechanical` role is the classifier,
and `classifierPrompt` (`tools.ts:902`) adds nothing but the schema name and the user's
request.

**On the trivial route the classifier, not the planner, authors `trivialItem.acceptance` —
and it is the one role the §3.2 budget governs that is never shown the rule.** So "not
following an instruction it has been given" is the wrong diagnosis here, and a
prompt-compliance fix aimed at the planner would miss it entirely.

### Why it decides the cell rather than costing a retry

Escalation is not a warning. `trivial` and `work` are the two routes priced in the step-1
budget section: 16 model calls (67% of T1) against ~47 (196%). Two acceptance rows opening
with `register(...)` and `get(...)` instead of `src/solvers/p001.py …` move the run from
the route that fits to the route that cannot. **At T1 the phrasing of two sentences decides
the outcome.**

It also generalises across the crawl rung rather than being one task's bad luck: every
`bench/corpus-euler.json` task registers through `src.registry`, whose module the prompt
forbids changing, so any faithful acceptance list is tempted toward exactly the bare-symbol
phrasing that costs a cluster.

### The fix, not applied here

One sentence in `classifierPrompt` — the §3.2 budget and the subject-first form — or the
same line lifted from `decompose.md` into the mechanical role's pack. It is a two-line
change and it is **deliberately not made in this session**: a cell was in flight, and the
working rule adopted above forbids editing `conductor/` while one is. It is the first thing
to do before any crawl-rung campaign, and its prediction is falsifiable in one cell — the
same prompt should classify `trivial` and stay there.

## The post-fix re-run — D10 removed, and the cell lost anyway

`step2-euler001-postfix`, 2026-08-26, same cell, D10 repaired and the router rebuilt. No
calibration reps were requested for this run.

**A noise-floor figure asserted here on first reading, and corrected:** step 1's baseline
spread was quoted as 1.10x off the two samples visible at the time. Step 1 wrote three
baseline cells, and across all five baseline samples now on disk the spread is **1.66x wall
(3.0-5.0 min) and 2.13x completion tokens (1,718-3,655)** — wider than epoch 14's four-task
baselines suggested and far wider than 1.10x. The separation from doctrine survives it:
doctrine's slowest baseline-beating margin is 9.4 min against a baseline maximum of 5.0, so
the ranges do not overlap. But "2.12x is real signal, not sampling" was asserted against a
denominator too small to support it, and the arithmetic is restated here rather than left
standing.

| arm | outcome | wall | completion tok | gauge |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| baseline | **pass** | 5.0 min | 3,655 | ran, passed |
| doctrine | **pass** | 11.6 min | 7,439 | ran, passed |
| conductor | **timeout** | 45.0 min | 24,090 | ran, failed |

### The fix worked, and it was checked rather than assumed

The classifier answered in one attempt with zero retries. That alone proves nothing — a
model that simply emitted valid JSON this time looks identical from the journal. Re-parsing
the recorded raw reply separates the two:

```
length: 1826
VERDICT: unparseable as sent (Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 1827)
ends inside string: False   unclosed: ['{']
```

**Unparseable as sent, short exactly one `}`, outside a string — the D10 signature for the
third time in two runs of this one cell**, at 1,346 / 1,565 / 1,826 characters. The repair
fired and recovered the verdict. D10's "n=1, did not recur" in the table above is stale;
it is frequent and looks length-correlated.

### And the cell lost anyway, twice to the same rule

```
13.9 min  guard-reject  classify   escalate-to-work
          "I1" spans 3 clusters (src/solvers/p001.py, register, get)
31.2 min  guard-reject  decompose
          "p001-solver" spans 3 clusters (p001.solve, src/solvers/p001.py, tests/check_p001.py)
```

This run never reached DECOMPOSED — worse than the pre-fix run, which did at 24.6 min. Two
planner waves, the second still generating at the ceiling.

The second rejection is the one that matters for what to do next. **The planner receives
`decompose.md`, which carries the subject-first instruction verbatim, and failed the rule
anyway.** So D45's remedy — showing the classifier the rule the planner already has —
addresses the 13.9-minute rejection and has no purchase on the 31.2-minute one.

`acceptance-cluster-defect.md` §8 (*What it still wrongly refuses*) already names this as
the accepted residual, and its own worked example shows a criterion **mentioning** a
testScope path folding correctly onto the declared file. What the planner did here is
different: it made `tests/check_p001.py` the criterion's *subject*. That is a genuine second
subject and the guard is right to count it. **The guard is correct, documented, repaired
twice, and the model does not reliably write single-subject criteria.**

### Where this leaves the crawl rung

`euler-001-py` has now been run three-arm four times and the conductor arm has lost every
time, with four different proximate causes — a cluster-extractor defect, the G8/§2.4 fork,
D10 into the work route, and the one-cluster budget firing at two stages. Baseline and
doctrine passed all four times, in 4.4–5.0 and 9.4–11.6 minutes.

**Step 3 is NO-GO on this evidence.** Sixty cells at roughly a day of wall clock would
reproduce a documented residual twenty times, which is the outcome the handoff's own second
step exists to prevent:

> A campaign that reproduces a known budget mismatch twenty times has bought nothing.

The blocker is not the budget and not a missing instruction. It is that the one-cluster
acceptance budget — correct as written — is not reliably satisfiable by this model at either
the classify or the decompose stage, and every euler task has the same shape that provokes
it. That is harness work with a falsifiable target, not a campaign.

## D45 fixed — and the planner's half was a wrong instruction, not a missing one

Two changes in `conductor/adapter/tools.ts`, both to pure prompt builders.

**The classifier now carries the rule.** `classifierPrompt` was 2,863 characters of schema
name plus the user's request; the `mechanical` role's only pack is `core.md`, which mentions
neither clusters nor criterion subjects. It now states the §3.2 budget, the subject-first
form, the preservation-guard escape, and a worked pair.

**The planner was told the wrong remedy.** `decomposePrompt`'s configured-limits line read:

> the per-item file cap: 5 files and one acceptance cluster; **split anything bigger.**

An item over budget because two criteria open with a bare symbol is not two items. Splitting
is the remedy for an item that covers two subjects; **rephrasing** is the remedy for one that
merely reads as though it does. `decompose.md:104` has the right advice, but it sits under
*Measured limits*, while the prompt quotes only the *Rejection checklist* section — so the
sentence the dispatch put in front of the planner contradicted the pack. That is D25's
"the planner is not following an instruction it has been given" turned on its head: it
followed the instruction it was given, and that instruction was wrong.

### The remedy was checked to be reachable before it was written

An early draft of this fix would have told the model to front every criterion with its
declared file. Run against the planner's actual rejected item, that is **not sufficient**:

```
AS WRITTEN                     -> ["p001.solve","src/solvers/p001.py","tests/check_p001.py"]
rows 0 and 5 subject-fronted   -> ["src/solvers/p001.py","tests/check_p001.py"]   still 2
```

Row 4 made the item's own test path the criterion's subject. Three phrasings do reach one
cluster, and the guidance names the one that generalises:

```
1 cluster   row 4 dropped
1 cluster   row 4 as a preservation guard      ("tests/check_visible.py is not modified")
1 cluster   row 4 fronted by the source file
```

**Advice that still fails the gate is worse than no advice**, because it converts a model
that cannot guess the convention into one that follows it and is refused anyway.

### The guard on the guidance

`ACCEPTANCE_SUBJECT_EXAMPLE` is one exported constant, quoted by both prompts, and
`doctrine-mechanics.test.ts` runs the **shipped** `acceptanceClusters` over both halves:

```
good -> ["src/parser.ts"]                            exactly one cluster
bad  -> ["parse","rejects","tests/parser.test.ts"]   genuinely refused
```

A prompt can state a rule correctly and hand the model an example the gate would refuse;
nothing in the prose shows it. The foil is there for the reason a guard needs a case it must
reject — an example that cannot be got wrong teaches nothing, and a row asserting only the
good half would pass over a vacuous one.

Gate: `GATE PASS` (2,064 node tests, up from 2,061), `M5 PASS`.

### The prediction, stated before the run

Same cell, same prompt: the classifier returns `trivial` and the item **survives** the §3.2
check, so the run advances to EXECUTING rather than escalating to `work`. That puts it on
the 16-call route — 67% of T1 — with the item pipeline still to pay for.

**This is not a prediction that the cell passes.** Classification consumed 10.5 minutes of
the last run for a one-word verdict, against the ~4 the 16-call model allows it. Surviving
the escalation is necessary and may well not be sufficient, and the honest falsifier is the
FSM state at the ceiling, not the gauge.

## D46 — D12's detector cannot fire on D12, and the register reads as covered

The D45 verification run's **doctrine** cell failed at 3.1 minutes on 499 completion tokens,
against 9.4 and 11.6 minutes and 5,939-7,439 tokens on the two runs before it. The
transcript:

```
→ Read src/registry.py
! permission requested: external_directory
    (/Users/sal/.llama-leash-work/llaacpp-qwen3.8-27b/none/doctrine/euler-001-py/r1/repo/src/*);
    auto-rejecting
✗ Read .../repo/src/cli.py failed
Error: The user rejected permission to use this specific tool call.
```

`llaacpp`. The real segment is `llamacpp` — **one character deleted**. opencode composed the
permission pattern from a corrupted copy of the work-root path, found the result outside the
project, and refused the doctrine arm a file in its own repository. It read four files, was
denied the fifth, and stopped.

**This is D12**, which `WORK_ROOT` in `run_and_watch.py` documents at eight missing
characters under `$TMPDIR`. Moving the work root to a short, stable, non-symlinked path made
it rarer; it did not remove it.

### The part that is new: the guard cannot see it

D12's row reads **`fixed (epoch 4)`** — *"A tool call denied on a path inside the cell's own
work tree is scored as an arm failure"*. `conductor_bench.denied_own_tree` implements it, and
run against this cell it returns **False**:

```
denied_own_tree -> False
denied path : .../llaacpp-qwen3.8-27b/none/doctrine/euler-001-py/r1/repo/src/*
cell tree   : .../llamacpp-qwen3.8-27b/none/doctrine/euler-001-py/r1/repo
exists?     : False
```

The detector's test is `candidate == tree or tree in candidate.parents`. **D12's mechanism is
a mangled path, and a mangled path is by construction never inside the tree.** The guard is
blind to the only defect it exists to catch.

Its own docstring argues the strictness, and the argument is sound in isolation:

> A refusal whose path cannot be read is therefore left alone: proving the path is inside the
> tree is required before anything is excluded.

That is right about the *cost* — `harness-error` excludes symmetrically, taking the other two
arms' cells for that task with it — and wrong about the *test*, because the shape it demands
is the one shape this defect cannot produce.

**A defect marked fixed whose detector cannot fire is worse than one marked open**, because
the register reads as covered and the next reader stops looking. Same family as D44 above:
the artifact that is checked is not the artifact that runs.

### The signature that is available

The denied path **does not exist on disk**, and differs from the real tree in exactly one
segment, where the mangled segment is a **subsequence** of the real one — characters deleted
and nothing else. That fits this one-character case and the eight-character case
`WORK_ROOT` records, and it stays conservative: a genuinely external path, a different arm's
tree (`baseline` is not a subsequence of `doctrine`) and a different task
(`euler-001-py` is not a subsequence of `euler-002-py`) all fail it.

Not implemented in this session: a cell was in flight, and the working rule above forbids
editing `scripts/` while one is.

### What it costs the measurement right now

This doctrine cell is scored `fail` / `passed: false` against the doctrine arm. It is not a
doctrine result — the arm was denied a file in its own repository by the harness. Any
per-arm pass rate computed over this run is wrong by one cell, in doctrine's disfavour, and
the crawl rung would have sixty chances to repeat it.

## D47 — a recalled constant becomes the item's contract, and nothing checks it

The `euler-001-py` transcripts carry the same integer three ways:

| value | occurrences across tonight's epochs | correct |
|---|---:|---|
| 233168 | 100 | yes |
| 233163 | 8 | no |
| 233166 | 4 | no |

**The answer is not in context.** Checked mechanically: it appears nowhere in the prompt,
nowhere in the ten-file seed, and `expected-answers.json` is not in the cell's repo. The
`gauge/` directory is materialized only after the arm's process exits. The value is coming
out of the weights — Project Euler 1 is among the most reproduced exercises in existence —
and the digit distribution is the signature of recalling a long numeral rather than looking
one up: the leading digits are stable, the tail is not.

### The baseline arm's handling, which is the design working

```
turn 3   "confirm that p001 resolves to 233166"                 <- wrong recall
turn 4   ran it, got 233168, and derived the closed form:
         3*333*334/2 = 166833   5*199*200/2 = 99500   15*66*67/2 = 33165
         166833 + 99500 - 33165 = 233168
         "I was misremembering 233166. Confirmed: 233168 is correct."
```

The anti-hardcode scan forbids writing the answer down, so the arm had to compute — and
computing corrected its own bad memory. That is exactly what `corpus-euler.json`'s
`whatThisMeasures` is for, and it held.

### The defect is one layer up, where nothing is looking

`whatThisMeasures` anticipates recall as a **scoring** worry — *"a model may recall the
answer without deriving it … what it cannot see is a derivation the model recalled whole"*.
What actually happened is a different failure. In the conductor arm the wrongly-recalled
value was written into the item's **acceptance criteria**, twice, in two separate classify
attempts:

> `"solve() computes the sum of integers below 1000 divisible by 3 or 5 (233163) without
> writing the value down"`

and the classifier reasoned itself into it deliberately:

> *"careful: the acceptance line is observable. The answer is 233163. But the constraint
> says the module must compute it, not write it down. The acceptance line can state the
> expected value."*

The reasoning is locally correct — an acceptance criterion SHOULD be observable and MAY
name an expected value. The problem is that the value is wrong and **no gate reads it.**

- The AST scan reads modules under `src/`. Acceptance rows live in `queue.json`.
- The hidden gauge validates the produced code against the verified answer. It never sees
  the criteria.
- `validateQueue` checks an item's shape, scope and cluster count. It has no notion of
  whether a criterion is TRUE.

So the constant is "written down" in the one place the anti-hardcode design was never
pointed at, and it becomes the contract the implementer builds to and the reviewer judges
against.

**Both failure directions are live.** Correct code can be refused for not matching a
poisoned criterion, or an item can be driven to GREEN against a criterion the hidden gauge
will then fail — and in the second case the arm reports success it does not have.

### Why this generalises past one task

Every task whose acceptance can name a computed value is exposed, and the euler corpus is
twenty of them. The wider shape is: **the harness validates artifacts and does not validate
the criteria it judges artifacts by.** A criterion is model output like any other, and it is
the only model output in the pipeline that nothing downstream checks.

Cheapest remedies, none implemented here:

- Forbid the classifier and planner from naming a numeric expected value in acceptance at
  all — the criterion `solve() computes the sum ... rather than writing the value down` is
  fully observable without the constant, and the constant adds nothing a test cannot state.
- Or treat a numeral in an acceptance row as a claim to be verified, which for this corpus
  means comparing it against the answer key the gauge already carries.

The first is a prompt rule and costs nothing. The second needs the grader's ground truth to
reach the planner, which the corpus deliberately withholds — so the first is the one that
fits the design.

**Prior art:** `prior_art.py recall` returns four unrelated hits. This is not recorded
anywhere, and `whatThisMeasures` anticipates the adjacent problem rather than this one.

## D45 verified — the conductor arm reaches VALIDATED and its gauge PASSES

`step3-euler001-d45`, same cell, D10 and D45 applied.

| arm | outcome | wall | completion tok | gauge |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| baseline | pass | 3.3 min | 2,133 | **passed** |
| doctrine | fail | 3.1 min | 499 | failed — **D46, not a doctrine result** |
| conductor | **timeout** | 45.0 min | 17,476 | **PASSED** |

### The prediction held exactly as written

The pre-registered falsifier was the FSM state, not the gauge: *"the classifier returns
`trivial` and the item survives the §3.2 check, so the run advances to EXECUTING rather
than escalating to `work`."*

```
 2.5 min  classifier dispatched
14.5 min  conductor_classify refused — the first dispatch hit the 12-min mechanical deadline
15.0 min  classifier re-dispatched
20.3 min  → trivial, attempt 1, zero retries
23.7 min  skeptic agrees; FSM → EXECUTING trivial      ← survived §3.2, first time in 5 runs
24.2 min  conductor_decompose refused from EXECUTING   ← D11 again
24.6 min  testWriter dispatched
31.9 min  FSM → RED
32.5 min  vet critic dispatched
38.6 min  FSM → TEST_VETTED
39.1 min  implementer dispatched
42.8 min  FSM → GREEN
43.3 min  FSM → VALIDATED

```

**Five of six item stages complete and the sixth in flight.** Against three previous runs
of this cell that reached DECOMPOSED at best and wrote zero bytes.

### What it produced

```python
from src.registry import register


def solve():
    return sum(n for n in range(1, 1000) if n % 3 == 0 or n % 5 == 0)


register("p001", solve)
```

`solve() = 233168`, registered, reachable through `get("p001")`, computed rather than

orchestrator planning and never writing** — the run that held the correct answer in a
compaction summary for twenty-six minutes and produced nothing.

### The accounting case the vocabulary was built for, arriving for the first time

`outcome=timeout` with `gauge.passed=true`. `conductor_bench`'s `GAUGE_KEYS` comment states
the design:

> `outcome` answers "did this arm deliver inside its wall clock"; `gauge` answers "was the
> work correct", and a cell that ran out of clock while holding a correct solution is the
> case that needs both.

Every prior timeout in this campaign held nothing, so that sentence has been a design note
for fourteen epochs. It is now data.

Note also **17,476 completion tokens against 27,636 and 24,090** in the two failed runs of
the same cell: it got further on fewer tokens, because the tokens stopped going to retries
and to the work route.

### What is still true

It timed out. The trivial route's floor is 67% of T1 and this run spent **45% of the budget
on classification alone** — 20.3 minutes for a one-word verdict, including a re-dispatch
after the first classifier turn exceeded its own 12-minute role deadline. That deadline
overrun is a cost D45 introduced: the guidance gives the classifier a rule to satisfy, and
it reasons longer for it.

So the honest reading is: **the pipeline works end to end on this task, and the intake half
consumes the budget the item half needs.** That is a different problem from the one this
cell had at the start of the session, and it is the next one.

### The three runs, side by side

| run | classify | branch | furthest state | produced | gauge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| step1 | 3 attempts, all unparseable | `work` | DECOMPOSED | nothing | fail |
| step2 | 1 attempt (D10 repair fired) | `work` | INTAKE, decompose rejected | nothing | fail |
| **step3** | 1 attempt (repair fired again) | **`trivial`** | **VALIDATED** | **correct code** | **PASS** |

Two two-line prompt changes separate the first row from the last.

---

## Intake costs 23.7 of 45 minutes, and the biggest line item is NOT a stall

Breakdown of the D45 verification cell's intake, from the journal's own clock:

| span | cost | what |
|---|---:|---|
| 0.0-2.5 | 2.5 min | orchestrator boot: one `bash` and five `read`s before it calls classify |
| **2.5-14.5** | **12.0 min** | classifier attempt 1 -> `subsession.abort` at the 12-minute `mechanical` deadline |
| 14.5-15.0 | 0.5 min | refusal, `conductor_status`, re-call |
| 15.0-20.3 | 5.3 min | classifier attempt 2 -> succeeds |
| 20.3-23.7 | 3.4 min | skeptic, including one JSON retry and its own `bash` + two `read`s |

**A reading asserted here on first look, and withdrawn one measurement later.** The router
ledger shows the aborted request as `completionTokens: null`, `upstreamMs: 720000`,
`timings: null`, and the session store agrees at `out_tokens=0`. Two independent sources
agreeing made "it generated nothing in twelve minutes" look established.

It is wrong, and this register already said why:

> The token count is zero because usage is written at completion and this turn never
> completed — not because nothing was produced.

The correct test is bytes over seconds, and it settles it:

| session | elapsed | reasoning bytes | rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| aborted `mechanical` | 720.7 s | 34,338 | **47.6 B/s (~12.5 tok/s)** |
| retry `mechanical` | 319.9 s | 14,948 | **46.7 B/s (~12.3 tok/s)** |

**Identical rates.** The killed sub-session was generating at the hardware's limit for the
whole twelve minutes and the axe fell mid-thought. That is the D43 finding reproduced —
*"every killed sub-session was generating at full speed"* — now at a fifth sighting and in
the `mechanical` role, which the earlier table did not have.

### So the intake problem is over-reasoning, not stalling

The two sessions produced the same verdict. One took 34,338 bytes of reasoning and died;
the other took 14,948 and answered. **The classifier spent 2.3x the reasoning the job needed
and lost all of it**, and a stall detector would have read it as healthy throughout, because
it was.

Two consequences:

- **D43 would not have saved these twelve minutes.** Recorded here rather than acted on;
  the tension it opens with — a stall deadline paired with an absolute ceiling re-creates
  the ceiling — is unchanged by this cell.
- **A suspect named here and cleared by the next comparison: the D45 guidance.** The
  reasoning is that classification went 10.5 minutes to 20.3 and the guidance is what
  changed. It does not survive the within-run numbers. **Both step-3 attempts used the
  SAME 3,788-character prompt** and took 12.0 minutes (aborted) and 5.3 minutes
  (succeeded) — and step 2's 10.5-minute success used the SHORTER 2,863-character prompt.
  The longer prompt's successful attempt was the FASTEST of the three. Reasoning length
  varies about 2.3x on identical input, and attributing that to the prompt is reading a
  spread as a trend.

- **What the numbers do support is that the deadline is calibrated for a different
  corpus.** `ROLE_TIMEOUT_MS` derives `mechanical: 720000` from 25 successes with a median
  of 3m29 and a slowest success of **6m10**, measured on `bench/conductor-tasks.json`.
  Against euler, three dispatches ran 5m18 (ok), 10m30 (ok) and >12m (killed) — one
  success already 70% past the slowest the calibration ever saw. The euler prompt is
  longer and denser than the ladder's, so the distribution the deadline was cut to fit is
  not the distribution it is now being applied to. That is D39's own rationale — *"a
  deadline cutting into the role's normal distribution rather than catching a pathology"* —
  recurring in the role D39 did not measure.

---

## D45b — the classifier stalled re-litigating the rule, not writing the item

The aborted classifier turn is readable, and its 34,338 bytes are not item authoring.
Its last words:

> "criterion 5 opens with `src/solvers/p001.py`, so it's the p001.py subject. Good. But it
> references `__init__.py`. Is that OK? … **Actually, wait. Let me reconsider.** Is there a
> risk the gate sees `src/solvers/__init__.py` in criterion 5 and counts it as a subject?"

The session that succeeded spent 13,499 bytes on the same job and ended *"the acceptance
criteria can be phrased to pass the gate. Let me write the final JSON."* Same work; one got
stuck simulating the gate.

**The worry is unfounded, and the guidance did not say so.** Measured against the shipped
`acceptanceClusters`:

| criterion shape | clusters |
|---|---:|
| opens with a declared path, names **another declared path later** | **1** |
| opens with a declared path, names a **test path later** | **1** |
| opens with a bare symbol | 1, named for the symbol |
| opens with an undeclared path, non-guard | 1, named for that path |
| opens with an undeclared path, guard phrasing | 0 |

So one clause answers it outright, and it is now in both prompts:

> ONLY THE FIRST PATH IN A CRITERION IS ITS SUBJECT. Naming other paths later in the same
> criterion costs nothing, so say what you mean and do not split a criterion to avoid
> mentioning a second file.

**A rule stated without the clause that resolves its obvious ambiguity buys deliberation,
not compliance** — and deliberation against a 12-minute role deadline is what killed the
turn. The clause is pinned by a row that runs the gate over the example rather than
asserting the prose, because telling a model something the gate does not do is worse than
telling it nothing.

Gate: `GATE PASS`, 2,066 node tests.

## Epoch 18 — pre-registered before the run: `grid2048-headless-py`, the first work-route cell

Three three-arm runs of `euler-001-py` exhausted what a single-item task can say. This is the
first cell aimed at the route the conductor exists for: **decompose → plan → plan review →
multi-item scheduling has never completed in 38 conductor cells**, and `PUBLISHED` and
`REPORTED` have never been reached at all.

`grid2048-headless-py` (T2, 60 min) is the smallest task that forces it: two requirements in
two files that already exist — the merge rule in `src/moves.py`, and undo's move-counter,
generator-state and CAPACITY handling in `src/undo.py` — with the rules in `SPEC.md` and no
plan in the prompt. Seed is green at 23 visible tests. Its gauge imports only seeded modules
and asserts against the specification's own pins, so unlike `snake-headless-py` it needs no
reseaming first.

**Predictions, recorded before launch:**

1. The classifier returns **`work`**, so `trivialItem` is null and the §3.2 acceptance-cluster
   gate is never consulted at intake. D45 and D45b are therefore NOT under test here.
2. Classification completes inside the 12-minute `mechanical` deadline. This is what D45b is
   under test for, and the falsifier is a `subsession.abort` at 720 s.
3. The run reaches **DECOMPOSED** and dispatches `conductor_plan`.
4. **It does not finish.** Measured cost is ~24 min intake plus ~25-30 min per item on the
   work route, against a 60-minute budget for two items. Reaching `PLANNED` with an item in
   flight would already be the furthest the work route has ever gone.

The value here is not pass/fail. It is that plan review, multi-item scheduling and the
dependsOn machinery have never run against a live model, and this cell is the cheapest thing
that makes them run.

### Baseline lands first, and it resets what "T2" means

| task | baseline wall | baseline completion tokens |
|---|---:|---:|
| `euler-001-py` (T1) | 3.3 min | 2,133 |
| `grid2048-headless-py` (T2) | **40.5 min** | **27,997** |

**12.3x the wall clock and 13.1x the tokens, for the arm with no plugin, no doctrine and no
fan-out.** It changed exactly the two files the prompt names plus the `NOTES.md` index — 55
insertions, 39 deletions — and its gauge passed. This is honest work at honest cost, not a
runaway.

Three things follow, and the third is the one that matters.

**The tier is a budget, not a difficulty rating, and the two have drifted apart.** T2 is
3,600 s. Baseline alone spends 68% of it. Every earlier reading of "the conductor arm is
13.6x baseline" was taken where baseline was three minutes; at forty it describes a cell
that cannot exist inside any budget this manifest declares.

**The euler rung was measuring a different difficulty class**, which the corpus said in its
own words and this is the first number attached to it:

> Registry plumbing, instruction-following across two files, and one computed integer …
> Read a high pass rate on this set as a statement about the harness, not about mathematics.

**Doctrine is now the interesting arm.** It has run 2-3x baseline all night, which puts it
at 80-120 minutes against a 60-minute ceiling. If it times out, that is the first cost
failure by the arm that has passed 13 of 14 epochs — and it would say the ceiling is
mis-set for this task rather than that any arm regressed.

### Doctrine costs 1.00x baseline here, and the campaign's cost claim is an artifact of task size

| task | baseline | doctrine | wall ratio | token ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `slugify-ts` | 3.7 min | 13.6 min | 3.70x | 4.17x |
| `euler-001-py` | 4.1 min | 10.5 min | 2.54x | 2.39x |
| `logfmt-lenses-ts` | 4.4 min | 17.6 min | 3.96x | 3.86x |
| `clock-inject-py` | 4.5 min | 11.7 min | 2.60x | 2.56x |
| `euler-cli-py` | 5.8 min | 14.9 min | 2.58x | 2.40x |
| **`grid2048-headless-py`** | **40.5 min** | **40.4 min** | **1.00x** | **0.99x** |

Averaged over every passing cell in every epoch on disk. Five tasks sit in a 3.7-5.8 minute
band and all of them cost doctrine 2.5-4.0x. The one task that takes forty minutes costs it
**nothing**.

**It is not an additive constant.** Fitting `doctrine = baseline + K` gives K = 6.4, 9.1,
9.9, 7.2 and 13.2 minutes on the five small tasks and **K = -0.1** on `grid2048`. Doctrine
does not add a fixed tax to real work; it has a **deliberation floor** — a minimum amount of
thinking the nine packs induce — and a forty-minute task has already exceeded it. Both arms
converge on the work the task requires, because the task is what defines the work.

**This reframes the campaign's most-repeated cost number.** *"Doctrine costs 3.4-7.4x
baseline wall clock"* was measured entirely on tasks where baseline finishes inside six
minutes. On the first task with real difficulty in this campaign, the multiplier is one —
and doctrine still beat baseline on `testQuality` 3 of 4 in epoch 14. The trade the register
has been describing, quality bought at several times the cost, **is not the trade on tasks
that are hard enough to need it.**

**n = 1 at the large size, and the claim is stated as one observation rather than a law.**
The falsifier is cheap and specific: a second task whose baseline exceeds thirty minutes
should also land near 1.0x. If it lands at 2.5x instead, this is a property of `grid2048`
and not of task size.

It also settles a question the crawl-before-walk handoff could not: **the euler rung was too
small to measure cost, not only too small to measure decomposition.** Every per-arm cost
ratio this campaign has published was taken in the band where doctrine's floor dominates.

### The conductor arm on the work route: intake is cheap, the PLANNER is the wall

Predictions 1 and 2 held, and the intake numbers are the opposite of what the euler cells
suggested:

```
 7.4 min  classifier dispatched          promptChars 3,987
 9.0 min  → work, attempt 1              1.6 min, zero retries, zero aborts
 9.0 min  skeptic dispatched
11.0 min  agrees, attempt 1              2.0 min
11.0 min  FSM → INTAKE work
14.2 min  planner dispatched             promptChars 15,117
34.2 min  *** ABORT ***                  exactly 20.0 min = the planner deadline
34.2 min  conductor_decompose REFUSED
34.3 min  planner re-dispatched          the same 15,117-char prompt
```

**Intake cost 11.0 minutes against euler's 23.7, and the classify call itself 1.6 minutes
against 5.3-12.0.** The reason is structural and it corrects the cost model the "fix intake
first" decision was built on: on the `work` route `trivialItem` is null, so **the classifier
never phrases acceptance criteria and therefore never simulates the cluster gate.** Every
minute of euler's expensive intake was rule-compliance deliberation on the trivial branch.
Intake is not a fixed ~24-minute tax; it is ~11 min on one branch and ~24 on the other.

D45b is confirmed on the branch it can be confirmed on: zero aborts, zero retries, zero
refusals through intake.

### The planner turn, measured rather than assumed

| turn | elapsed | reasoning bytes | tools | rate |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 1 | 183.5 s | 4,055 | bash, glob | 22.6 B/s |
| 2 | 25.8 s | 61 | read x4 | — |
| **3** | **990.8 s** | **49,226** | none | **49.7 B/s (~13.1 tok/s)** |

**16.5 minutes of unbroken generation at the hardware's single-stream decode rate, cut
mid-sentence.** This is the register's D43 finding at a sixth sighting and the first on the
work route: the killed session was not stalled, it was thinking, and a liveness signal would
have read it as healthy throughout — correctly.

Two things separate it from the euler classifier stall. It emitted **49 KB in one unbroken
block with no self-interruption**, where the classifier looped re-reading one clause; and it
carries a **15,117-character prompt**, roughly twice the size the planner's 1,200,000 ms
deadline was calibrated against. A larger planning problem, stated at greater length, worked
serially — not confusion.

**The first work-route cell therefore says the binding constraint is not intake.** Intake
was clean and cheap. What does not fit is a real decomposition inside the planner's
deadline, and a re-dispatch buys another 20 minutes of the same against a 60-minute ceiling
that has 25 left.

### Why the planner deliberates so long: its prompt is the repository

`decomposePrompt` ends with `scopableFilesSection`, which inlines the FULL CONTENTS of every
scopable file:

> "The files those globs own, with their current contents — this is the whole of what they
> hold, so decompose from here rather than reading them again"

That is the fix for roles re-deriving context they were never given (D16/D26/D29 family), and
on this cell it plainly worked: the planner made four `read`s and one `bash`, then stopped
touching the repo and reasoned. It also means **the planner's prompt is a fixed ~4.5 KB plus
the entire `src/` tree.**

| task | `src/` bytes inlined | live planner prompt | planner outcome |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `euler-001-py` | 1,685 | 6,169 | completed in 8.4 min |
| `grid2048-headless-py` | 9,532 | **15,117** | **aborted at 20.0 min, twice** |

2.45x the prompt, at least 2.4x the deliberation — roughly linear.

**And the deadline it is measured against was calibrated on the smaller distribution.**
`ROLE_TIMEOUT_MS`'s own comment gives the planner's basis as 28 dispatches, median 7m48,
slowest success 13m38 — every one of them on `bench/conductor-tasks.json`, whose seed repos
are the small ones. A deadline cut to fit a ~6 KB-prompt distribution is now being applied to
a 15 KB prompt. **That is the same defect as the `mechanical` deadline finding earlier in
this session, one role over**, and it is D39's rationale — *"a deadline cutting into the
role's normal distribution rather than catching a pathology"* — recurring for the third time.

Two levers, and they pull against each other:

- **Scale the per-role deadline with prompt size** rather than pinning one number per role.
  Cheap, and it keeps the inlining that removed the re-reading.
- **Inline less** — only the files the decomposition will plausibly touch. Smaller prompt,
  shorter deliberation, and it reintroduces exactly the re-reading the inlining was built to
  stop.

Neither is chosen here. What this cell establishes is that the work route's binding
constraint is **the planner's deadline against a prompt that scales with the repository**,
and not intake, which cost 11 clean minutes.

### DECOMPOSED, first time on the work route — and the decomposition is good

The re-dispatched planner answered at 45.6 min, attempt 1, and the run reached **DECOMPOSED
with three items**:

| item | fileScope | testScope | behavioral | dependsOn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `merge-r7` | `src/moves.py` | `tests/check_merge.py` | yes | — |
| `undo-r13-r14` | `src/undo.py` | `tests/check_undo.py` | yes | — |
| `notes-index` | `NOTES.md` | — | **no** | both of the above |

**No `guard-reject` anywhere in this run.** All three items pass the one-cluster budget —
10, 10 and 3 acceptance rows, one cluster each — where step 2's euler decompose was rejected
for exactly this:

```
1 cluster(s)  merge-r7       ["src/moves.py"]   rows: 10
1 cluster(s)  undo-r13-r14   ["src/undo.py"]    rows: 10
1 cluster(s)  notes-index    ["NOTES.md"]       rows: 3
```

**D45 and D45b are visibly working on the planner, not merely present.** Every preservation
row is in the taught form — `src/rng.py is not modified`, `src/board.py is not modified` —
and every deliverable row opens with the declared file. Ten rows folding to one cluster is
the rule obeyed rather than dodged: the planner stated MORE behaviour than a two-row item
would and still passed.

The plan is also right about things the prompt did not spell out:

- It found a **third** item. The prompt says `NOTES.md` keeps the index of which requirement
  is where; the planner made maintaining that index its own item.
- It marked that item `behavioral: false` with an empty testScope, which is the correct
  shape for a documentation change and is a §2.4 rule it could have failed.
- It gave it `dependsOn: ["merge-r7", "undo-r13-r14"]` — the index cannot be marked done
  before the work is.
- The two implementation items are independent, matching the prompt's own *"They touch
  different files and neither depends…"*.
- Its acceptance cites real spec rows — R7 step 2, R9's twelve-row table, R13's move counter
  and generator state, CAPACITY, R14 — with concrete cases like `[4,4,8,0]` and the
  no-double-merge row.
- Both test paths match the runner's `check_*.py` glob, so they are reachable — the hazard
  that wedged two epoch-14 cells.

**This is the campaign's thesis appearing as an artifact rather than an argument.** Baseline
solved the same task in 40.5 minutes by editing two files directly, and produced no plan, no
dependency order and no acceptance criteria at all — because nothing asked it to. Whether
that plan is worth its cost is the open question; that the harness produces one, on a task
with real difficulty, is no longer in doubt.

It arrived at minute 45.6 of 60, with `conductor_plan` — another planner call against a
20-minute deadline — still ahead of it.

### Epoch 18 final — and the conductor arm now loses to arithmetic, not to a defect

| arm | outcome | wall | prompt tok | completion tok | gauge | produced |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| baseline | **pass** | 40.5 min | 557,783 | 27,997 | **passed** | working code |
| doctrine | **pass** | 40.4 min | 960,591 | 27,604 | **passed** | working code |
| conductor | **timeout** | 60.0 min | 514,852 | 16,720 | failed | **nothing** |

The conductor timed out inside `conductor_plan`, at DECOMPOSED, holding a correct three-item
decomposition and an empty diff.

**The prompt-token column explains the doctrine result mechanically.** Doctrine sends 1.72x
baseline's prompt tokens and 0.99x its completion tokens, and finishes in the same wall
clock — which is the euler-001 forensics' rule holding exactly:

> Prompt volume does not set wall clock on this rig; completion volume does.

The nine packs prefill and cache; they are nearly free in time. What cost 2.5-4.0x on the
small tasks was never the prompt — it was the extra DELIBERATION the doctrine induces, and a
forty-minute task has already paid for that deliberation on its own account.

**Where the 60 minutes went:**

| span | cost | what |
|---|---:|---|
| 0.0-7.4 | 7.4 min | orchestrator boot — reads before calling classify |
| 7.4-11.0 | 3.6 min | classify + skeptic, one attempt each, no retries |
| 14.2-34.2 | **20.0 min** | planner attempt 1 — aborted on its deadline, 49 KB of reasoning discarded |
| 34.3-45.6 | 11.3 min | planner attempt 2 — DECOMPOSED, 3 items |
| 48.6-60.0 | 11.4 min | `conductor_plan` — still generating at the ceiling |

**Two thirds of the budget went to planning, and a third of it to one discarded attempt.**
Nothing in this cell was a guard misfiring, a schema failure, a wrong branch or a stall.
Every stage that ran, ran correctly.

That is a different position from the one this campaign has been in for fourteen epochs. The
conductor arm is no longer losing to defects on this task; it is losing to the fact that
**planning a real change costs more wall clock than making it.** Baseline made the change in
40.5 minutes. The conductor spent 45.6 producing a plan of it and had 14 left to execute
three items.

Whether that trade is ever worth taking is the campaign's actual question, and this is the
first cell that poses it cleanly.
