# Epoch 19 — the deadlines come off, because the distribution was never observed

## Why, and why it is a measurement rather than a concession

A deadline can only be sized against a distribution somebody has seen. This one has never
been seen. `ROLE_TIMEOUT_MS`'s calibration table records **39% of planner dispatches killed**
— and a killed roll never reveals how long it would have taken, so every figure in that table
is a lower bound on a right-censored sample. Six sightings across this campaign show the
killed session generating at the hardware's full rate and cut mid-sentence; **not one shows a
deadline catching a pathology.**

The instrument was removing the measurement. The only way to size the tail is to stop
truncating it.

This also matches what the harness is FOR. It exists to test whether structured planning buys
correctness on the first try, with time and tokens as the declared price. Measuring that under
artificial time pressure confounds the thing being measured.

## What is off, what is still on

| layer | was | now | why |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `ROLE_TIMEOUT_MS` (all three roles) | 720-1200 s | **21,600,000 ms (6 h)** | effectively off |
| `SUB_SESSION_TIMEOUT_MS` | 900 s | **21,600,000 ms** | effectively off, unlisted roles |
| `ROUTER_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_MS` | 600 s | **7,200,000 ms** | a wave queued behind long generations would otherwise be REFUSED while waiting, reporting as a router error rather than as the long turn it is |
| `grid2048` T2 budget | 3,600 s | **28,800 s (8 h)** | the single outer bound |
| `router.hpp kRelayTimeoutSeconds` | 600 s | **unchanged** | see below |
| `verify.scopes.repo.timeoutMs` | the cell budget | **600,000 ms fixed** | see below |

**This is not "no timeouts", and the distinction is the whole safety argument.**
`kRelayTimeoutSeconds` is a **per-read** timeout on the relay, not a total: a session that
keeps emitting never trips it, and a session that genuinely stops emitting dies after 600 s
of silence. That is a LIVENESS signal, which is the correct shape for catching a hang, and it
has never fired on healthy work. What comes off is the DURATION guard, which has killed
healthy work six times and caught nothing.

The cell budget stays as the one outer bound because it is the only thing that stops a run
looping inside the FSM, where every turn emits tokens and the relay guard therefore never
sees silence.

Deadlines are spelled as literals rather than a named constant in `conductor_wiring.py`:
`conductor/tests/composition.test.ts` parses that file and compares the numbers against
`config-io.ts`'s mirror, and a named constant reads better while defeating a real
cross-language drift check.

## R5, fixed — and raising the budget is what made it urgent

`verify.scopes.repo.timeoutMs` was `run_timeout_sec * 1000`: the cell's ENTIRE wall clock,
handed to a command that runs a unit suite in milliseconds (grid2048's visible suite is 23
tests in 0.001 s). Merely silly at a 45-minute cell. At an eight-hour cell it is a hung
subprocess's licence to eat the whole run.

**A verify is not a model call.** It is a local process that finishes in seconds or is broken,
which makes it the one deadline in this configuration worth keeping — and it must not be
derived from the budget it exists to protect. It is now a fixed 600,000 ms, with two rows
pinning that it does not track the cell budget and that it stays inside a sane band.

That is R5 from the euler-001 forensics, open since 2026-08-21 and closed here.

## What is being watched, since the guard that used to watch is off

Two signatures, sampled every two minutes from the journal and the session store:

- **the loop** — the same wave role dispatched four or more times, which is the FSM retrying
  a refused tool. This is the real risk of removing duration deadlines: every turn emits
  tokens, so the relay's silence guard cannot see it.
- **the stall** — reasoning bytes flat across four consecutive samples on a live turn. This
  is D43's own signal, hand-run rather than built, and D43 remains reserved for its own
  session.

## Carried over rather than re-measured

`baseline` and `doctrine` are reused from epoch 18 rather than re-run. Both arms load no
plugin, so nothing in this configuration change can reach them, and both finished at ~40.5
minutes against a 60-minute cap that never bound them. The driver's own resume path does
this and announces it: *"this results directory already holds scored cells; those cells will
be REUSED and not re-run."* It puts eighty minutes into the cell that is actually under test.

## A live stall signal that works, found by building the one the register warned about

Watching epoch 19 with the duration guard off, a hand-rolled detector fired at 28.8 min:
reasoning bytes in `opencode.db` flat at 38,824 across four samples. It was wrong. At that
moment:

```
llama-server   113.0% cpu      <- generating
opencode        21.9% cpu
journal tail:  28.8 min  inject/system-append (planner)
```

The planner was mid-turn and healthy. **Parts for an in-flight message are not flushed to the
store until the message completes**, so a live poller reads flat bytes through an entirely
normal turn. The euler-001 measurement worked only because it read the session AFTER an abort
had finalized it.

This is the trap the D43 section already records, built by the same reader who quoted it:

> The signal D43 wants to calibrate against is not in the archive — and its available proxy
> is a trap. `opencode.db`'s `event` table holds 474 session-lifecycle rows and no part
> deltas.

**The signal that does work needs no part stream**, and both halves are already on the wire:

- **the journal**, whose `inject/system-append` record marks a request assembled and
  dispatched. The euler-001 forensics established the reading — *"a gap that begins at an
  inject is the model generating"* — and verified it against all twelve of that cell's
  largest gaps.
- **llama-server's CPU**, which is ~113% while decoding and near zero while idle.

A run is generating when the journal's last record is an inject and the server is busy. It is
stalled when the journal is quiet after an inject and **the server is idle**. That is a
liveness signal derived from two things every run already produces, it needs no `message.
part.updated` stream, and it costs one `ps` and one file read to sample.

Handed to the D43 session rather than acted on here. What it does not settle is D43's own
stated tension — that pairing a stall deadline with an absolute ceiling re-creates the
ceiling — and this epoch is the first evidence about the other half of that question, since
it is running with the ceiling effectively removed.

## Epoch 19 result — the deadlines came off and worked; the budget did not come off at all

| arm | outcome | wall | completion tok | gauge |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| baseline | pass | 40.5 min | 27,997 | passed *(carried from epoch 18)* |
| doctrine | pass | 40.4 min | 27,604 | passed *(carried from epoch 18)* |
| conductor | **timeout** | **60.0 min** | **30,634** | failed |

```
 4.2 min  classifier dispatched
 5.7 min  → work (1.5 min)
 8.0 min  FSM → INTAKE
 9.8 min  planner dispatched
22.6 min  FSM → DECOMPOSED, 3 items      planner roll: 12.8 min, NO ABORT
24.3 min  conductor_plan dispatched
48.9 min  still generating                24.6+ min, NO ABORT
60.0 min  cell ceiling
```

**The role-deadline removal did exactly what it was for.** Zero aborts, zero refusals, and
`conductor_plan` ran **24.6+ minutes** where the old 20-minute deadline would have killed it
at minute 44.3. Completion tokens went 16,720 → **30,634** in the same 60 minutes: 1.8x more
real work, because none of it went to a discarded attempt.

**And the first uncensored planner roll is 12.8 minutes** — INSIDE the old 20-minute limit.
So the deadline was never cutting the median; it was cutting the slow third. Its damage was
probabilistic rather than systematic: roughly one planner call in three died, and each death
cost the full twenty minutes plus a re-dispatch, on a route that makes two such calls.

The loop signature never fired. Removing the duration guard did not produce FSM looping.

### The budget change did not apply, and the readout said it had

`bench/corpus-games.json` raised `defaults.tierTimeoutSec.T2` to 28,800. The cell died at
exactly 3,600 s. The task carries its own override:

```
timeout = entry.get("runTimeoutSec", tier_timeouts[tier])     # conductor_bench.py:990
grid2048-headless-py | tier T2 | runTimeoutSec = 3600         # and it wins
```

**This is D44's shape a third time** — change the representation you find first, never check
the one the system reads. What makes it worse than a plain slip is that `run_and_watch`
printed **"worst case 24.0 hours"**, computed from the tier table, so the change looked
applied while the driver used a different number entirely. *A confirming readout drawn from
the wrong source is worse than no readout.*

The check costs one line and is the value the driver itself parses, not the table it falls
back to:

```
$ python3 -c "...; m = cb.load_manifest('bench/corpus-games.json'); ..."
  grid2048-headless-py   tier=T2   EFFECTIVE run_timeout_sec=28800 (8.0 h)
```

So epoch 19 measured the role deadlines correctly and the budget not at all. The rerun below
carries the same configuration with the override fixed.

## conductor_plan does not terminate in this configuration, and the deadline was hiding that

Epoch 20 let the plan stage run with no role deadline. After 160 minutes, measured from the
router ledger over the planner's own requests:

```
compactions (prompt drops) : 6
output-cap hits (=16384)   : 4
peak prompt tokens         : 51,833     threshold = 65536 - 16384 = 49,152
completion tokens spent    : 122,654    (~151 min of decode at 13.5 tok/s)
```

**122,654 completion tokens — 4.4x baseline's entire budget for the whole task (27,997) —
and no artifact.**

The cycle is stable. Each lap climbs past 49,152 prompt tokens, gets compacted, re-reads the
tree, rebuilds the same reasoning, reaches the emit step, and is truncated at the 16,384
output cap. The session store shows the shape plainly: turns 6, 7 and 12 each end within a
sentence of emitting the JSON, and turns 9-11 and again at 152-157 min are re-derivation
after a compaction — twenty `read`s and three `bash` calls to reconstruct a tree the
decompose stage was handed inline.

**The reasoning is not the problem.** Every thinking block is on the right concepts:
`slide_left`'s merge walk, the R9 twelve-row table, widening the snapshot to
`(grid, score, moves, rng_state)`, CAPACITY enforcement, and verifying no other module
touches the snapshot internals. There is no wandering and no confusion. It is being defeated
by its containers.

### What this changes about three earlier epochs

Epochs 18, 19 and 20's predecessors all recorded `timeout at conductor_plan`. That was the
right outcome with the wrong cause attached: the stage was not slow and about to finish, and
the 20-minute deadline was not clipping a tail. **The stage does not terminate**, and the
deadline was converting a non-terminating stage into a timeout that looked like a budget
problem. Removing the deadline did not let it finish — it revealed that it cannot.

### And it settles the change-set ordering empirically

`docs/plans/2026-08-27-making-the-plan-stage-affordable.md` ranks shrinking the plan artifact
first on the grounds that it is the largest lever. This measurement is stronger than that:
**it is the only lever that changes the outcome.** Speculative decoding at 2x buys twelve
failed laps instead of six. `--parallel 1` buys slightly cheaper failed laps. The artifact
`plan.md` is required to carry — complete code for every non-obvious step, for a change that
is two functions — is what does not fit, and nothing downstream of it matters until it does.

The run continues to the 8-hour cap by choice, because the lap count, the final token total
and whether the item pipeline is ever reached are all worth having measured rather than
inferred.

### The six-hour measurement: conductor_plan is a closed loop, and no budget exits it

The role deadlines were set to 21,600,000 ms with the note that no healthy roll could reach
six hours. **A single `conductor_plan` dispatch reached it exactly**, and the claim that it
was unreachable is withdrawn:

```
 44.6 min  conductor_plan dispatched
404.6 min  *** ABORT *** {"reason":"watchdog-timeout","timeoutMs":21600000}
           360.0 minutes, one dispatch, no artifact
404.6 min  REFUSED conductor_plan: "the planner sub-session produced no valid Plan"
408.4 min  re-dispatched
```

Measured over that dispatch's own requests in the router ledger:

| | |
|---|---:|
| compactions (prompt drops) | **16** |
| output-cap hits, exactly 16,384 | **9** |
| peak prompt tokens | 51,833 *(threshold 49,152)* |
| completion tokens | **397,154** |
| at 13.5 tok/s | **8.2 hours of decode** |
| against baseline's ENTIRE task | **14.2x** |

**Sixteen laps.** Each climbed past the compaction threshold, was compacted, re-read the
tree, rebuilt the same reasoning, reached the emit step, and was truncated. Nine got far
enough to hit the output cap. The stage spent fourteen times the cost of the whole solution
failing to write a plan for it, and would have continued indefinitely.

**This is what six uninterrupted hours bought that no shorter run could.** Under any deadline
below six hours the stage reports `timeout`, which reads as a budget problem and invites the
wrong fix. Running it to exhaustion makes it undeniable that **no budget exits this loop**.
The 20-minute deadline was not wrong about when to stop; it was wrong about what it was
stopping, and three epochs recorded the symptom as the cause.

It also makes the change set in
`docs/plans/2026-08-27-making-the-plan-stage-affordable.md` absolute rather than relative.
Speculative decoding at 2x yields thirty-two failed laps instead of sixteen. `--parallel 1`
yields slightly cheaper failed laps. **Only shrinking the artifact the stage must emit
changes the outcome**, and the artifact is oversized by specification — `plan.md`'s own
self-check requires complete code for every non-obvious step, for a change that is two
functions in two files.

## Epoch 20 final — eight hours, 307k tokens, an empty diff

| arm | outcome | wall | prompt tok | completion tok | gauge | produced |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| baseline | **pass** | 40.5 min | 557,783 | 27,997 | **passed** | working code |
| doctrine | **pass** | 40.4 min | 960,591 | 27,604 | **passed** | working code |
| conductor | **timeout** | **480.0 min** | 2,327,452 | **307,031** | failed | **nothing** |

The conductor tree at the cap is byte-identical to the seed apart from the harness's own
`gauge/`. **11x baseline's entire completion budget, and an empty diff.**

```
  7.1 min  classifier
 11.5 min  FSM -> INTAKE (work)
 13.9 min  planner #1 -> 13.5 min -> GUARD-REJECT decompose
 27.4 min  planner #2 -> 13.7 min -> 3 items, correct dependsOn
 41.1 min  FSM -> DECOMPOSED
 44.6 min  conductor_plan
404.6 min    *** ABORT *** 21,600,000 ms — 360.0 minutes, 16 laps, no artifact
408.4 min  conductor_plan re-dispatched
480.0 min  cell cap
```

**It reached a correct three-item plan at minute 41 and spent the next 439 minutes failing to
write down how to execute it.** 90% of an eight-hour run was one stage that cannot terminate.

### What worked, which localises the defect

Intake was 11.5 minutes and clean — no retries, no aborts. Decompose produced two planner
rolls at 13.5 and 13.7 minutes, one guard-reject correctly caught and recovered from, and
three well-formed items with correct `dependsOn` ordering and disjoint scopes. **Everything
up to the plan stage is functional and affordable.** The failure is one stage and one
artifact, not the architecture.

### The comparison the campaign exists to make, on work with real difficulty

Baseline and doctrine both solved this task in ~40 minutes with near-identical completion
counts. Doctrine sent 1.72x the prompt tokens and 0.99x the completion tokens and finished in
the same wall clock, because the packs prefill and cache and wall clock is set by completion.
**Doctrine is free on real work.** The conductor spent 11x and produced nothing.

That is the campaign's central claim tested against a task hard enough to need it, and it
fails — for a reason now identified precisely enough to fix:
`docs/plans/2026-08-27-making-the-plan-stage-affordable.md`, §4.1.

## D48 — the plan stage terminates, epoch 21

`docs/plans/2026-08-27-making-the-plan-stage-affordable.md` §4.1 and §4.2, applied and
re-measured on the same cell (`grid2048-headless-py`, `qwen3.8-27b` Q6_K, M4 Max 64 GB,
results at `.data/benchmark/watch/step7-plan-terminates`, run `r-20260827-9832`). Baseline
and doctrine were reused from the step-4 directory — neither loads the plugin, so no change
here can reach them.

### The one stage that had never completed

| `conductor_plan` | epoch 20 | epoch 21 |
|---|---:|---:|
| wall clock | 360.0 min, then a 6h watchdog | **22.0 min** |
| dispatch attempts | re-dispatched, then the cell cap | **1** |
| compactions inside the dispatch | 16 | **0** |
| output-cap hits at exactly 16,384 | 9 | **0** |
| peak prompt tokens | 51,833 (threshold 49,152) | **28,478** |
| completion tokens | 307,031 | **6,356** |
| artifact | none — tree byte-identical to the seed | **`plan.md`, 5,343 B, 4 decision records** |
| FSM | stuck at `DECOMPOSED` | **`-> PLANNED`** |

Whole run to `PLANNED`: 49 minutes and **12,719 completion tokens**, against a plan stage
alone that previously spent 307,031 and returned nothing. The one suspected compaction in the
run belongs to the intake skeptic, not the planner.

### What the two changes did, separately

**§4.1 — `conductor/doctrine/plan.md` rule 3 and its self-check.** The rule demanded complete
code for every non-obvious step, so `plan.md` had to carry the solution before the implementer
wrote it. It now demands code only where the item's `acceptance` and `testScope` leave a real
choice open — an algorithm whose shape is a judgment call, a seam neither item's acceptance
pins, a value decided once and not re-derivable — and elsewhere the step names its path, its
symbol and its change and stops.

The artifact shows the narrowing landing exactly where it was aimed. `merge_rule` step 2
carries the full merge walk, because SPEC's twelve-row table pins the *output* of that
algorithm and not its *shape*; step 1 describes the test file in prose, because the item's
acceptance already is that specification. The plan is 5,343 B against a diff of comparable
size, where epoch 20's was specified larger than the window that had to hold it.

**§4.2 — `planPrompt` carries the scopable tree**, as `decomposePrompt` has since D36. The
brief went 6,828 -> 17,197 chars. The planner's plan turn made **no tool call at all** — it
answered directly, where epoch 20 spent 20 `read`s and 3 `bash`es *per lap*, paid once per
compaction rather than once per run.

**One addition beyond the plan document:** the brief now states that the reply is one message
under a hard cap and that overrunning it loses the whole dispatch rather than its tail. A
planner truncated at exactly 16,384 tokens nine times had never been told a wall existed.
Relaxing the doctrine makes a short plan possible; naming the wall is what makes one likely.

### The cost, and where it was paid from

`conductor/tests/doctrine-mechanics.test.ts` caps every doctrine pack at 7,000 bytes, and its
comment is explicit that a pack pushing against the ceiling is a pack to cut. The first draft
of the narrowed rule came in at 7,562 B and went red, so the rule paid for itself out of prose
it made redundant: the per-item test-strategy line, the placeholder section's closing
paragraph, and two rationale clauses. `plan.md` is 6,960 B.

Four `[D48]` tests pin the change and were verified red against the pre-change sources by
stashing them: the retired unconditional sentence is absent from the pack; the narrowing
survives the `doctrineSlice` into the dispatch brief; the brief names the reply cap; and the
brief carries the source under the receiving stage's own verb.

`planRevisionPrompt` deliberately carries no tree: it is the widest prompt the planner ever
sees, and the standing plan it already carries names by path every file a revision touches.

### What this does not yet say

`PLANNED` is not a passing gauge. This measures the stage that had never produced an artifact,
and nothing downstream of it. *(Correction, epoch 22: plan review has since been measured on
this task twice — see D49. The dispatch wave has been entered but never completed — see D50.)*

## D49 — every plan-review lens re-derives the repository, and half of them die trying

Epoch 21's plan review ran 4h28m before its operator killed it; its first round spent ~21 of
its first 26 minutes on `read` calls, four lenses re-reading the same tree independently, then
compacted and truncated mid-JSON on two lenses of four. The change (shipped with epoch 22's
launch, `[D49]` tests in `conductor/tests/doctrine-mechanics.test.ts`): `handlePlanReview`
reads the scopable tree ONCE before the round loop and every `lensPrompt` carries it inline,
the same D36 treatment `planPrompt` got in D48; and the lens brief now states the one-message
hard cap and asks for claim/evidence/fix without the reasoning that produced them.

Measured, epoch 22 (run r-20260828-c828): plan review completed in ONE round where epoch 21
took its whole 4h28m without finishing — and the round surfaced a real major (a wave that
contradicts its own dependsOn ordering). Lens turns made zero read calls.

## D50 — a dispatched test-writer asked a question no one exists to answer, and the gate said yes

The terminal event of epoch 22's conductor cell. Journal seq 140 of 140:
`gates/allow {toolName: "question", toolClass: "read", sideEffect: "R0"}` for the test-writer
session `ses_fb8778b94ffe…`. The console's last frame is 78.7 minutes later with no matching
completion, no ledger row, no llama-server task — the session was parked on an operator answer
in a headless `opencode run` cell, at zero GPU, until the driver was killed. All three queue
items were still PENDING; the arm produced no scored cell.

The cause is a three-layer chain, each layer verified against its artifact:

1. **The tool is client-gated, not registry-only.** wire-notes 20.1 recorded `question` as
   "not offered", measured by deepEqual — against the non-cli fixture client. Read from the
   1.18.15 binary itself: `ro=["app","cli","desktop"].includes(i.client)||i.enableQuestionTool`
   then `...ro?[_.question]:[]`. `opencode run` is the cli client, so every benchmark cell
   offers the tool the wire contract says does not exist.
2. **The fragment re-opened what the base ruleset closes.** opencode's own base narrowing
   carries `question * -> deny`; `conductor/opencode-fragment.json` overrode it to
   `"question": "ask"` on all six subagents — deliberately, so the plugin's permission handler
   could see and refuse the ask.
3. **That handler is unreachable.** Across epochs 21 and 22 — two full runs, nine dispatched
   sub-sessions — the journal holds ZERO permission-bearing records. The event router requires
   a `permission` string on the payload and bails silently without one, and the payload shape
   was verified once, for an `edit` ask, on 2026-08-12. The grant-then-refuse design never
   fired even once, and nothing recorded that it had not.

The fix closes the surface at every layer and reverses the fragment's theory: the tool is
REMOVED rather than granted-and-refused. `tools.question: false` on all seven agents (the
measured two-layer closure: omitted from the offered set AND a deny rule emitted);
`adapter/tools.ts` refuses the tool at the gate as the latent-surface pin, classified write so
a gate crash fails closed; and the refusal deliberately does NOT name `NEEDS_CONTEXT` — the
observed call was a degenerate end-of-turn ask from a session whose work was already complete
(`{"header":"noop","question":"Placeholder — returning ImplementerResult directly."}`), and
steering such a session toward "blocked" would convert a finished item into a stuck one. The
silent bail now journals `state/permission.unhandled` naming the payload keys it saw.

Two adjacent defects fixed under the same number, both of the stale-artifact class:
`apply_conductor_wiring` deep-merged the fragment over a base config that carries the wiring
too, so a key REMOVED from the fragment survived in every generated config forever — agent
definitions are consumed verbatim now, replacing the base entry wholesale. And
`fragment.test.ts`'s "grant question so the plugin can refuse it" assertion is inverted: the
refusal path it was written to serve is structurally dead on this build.

Predicted effect, stated honestly: unblocking the executor RESUMES the cell toward its
480-minute budget — epoch 20 ran the same task the full 480 minutes with zero question calls
and an empty diff, so this removes the one failure mode that yields no data at all, and it
will INCREASE the conductor arm's decode, not decrease it.

## D51 — a provider timeout journaled as the model's schema failure

Epochs 21-22 show eleven router-ledger rows with status 200, upstreamMs 1,800,018-1,804,979
and every token field null — 1:1 with eleven `JSON Parse error: Unexpected EOF` events. The
provider abandons the generation at its 1,800 s ceiling and reports it ON the assistant
message (`info.error: {"name":"UnknownError","data":{"message":"The operation timed out."}}`)
inside a 200 envelope, with a reasoning part and NO text part. `extractReplyText` composes
`""`, `JSON.parse("")` is exactly that EOF, and fanout journaled `schema-invalid` — a lie
about the model's output that sent this campaign chasing a prompt fix, and whose re-prompt
appended "Correct these validation errors" feedback about a reply that was never delivered,
growing the prompt that had just timed out.

The fix reads `info.error` in the failure path — AFTER the receipt check, so a reply that
both errored and validated is still honoured — journals `provider-error` carrying the
provider's own message, re-prompts with the ORIGINAL brief, and bounds provider errors at two
attempts: measured across both journals, six of eight lenses that hit the timeout returned a
valid receipt on the very next attempt and none recovered later. The retry itself stays —
removing it would have converted three completed plan-review waves into hard aborts and
deleted 17,024 tokens of real lens output from epoch 22 alone. The retry record now carries
the response text, so settling the next dispute of this kind needs no database read.

## D52 — an eight-day-old router config governed the run

`serve.py --no-shell` os.execv's into llama-server BEFORE its own `write_router_config`
runs, and `run_and_watch.start_services` handed the supervisor whatever
`.data/configs/conductor-router.json` was on disk — mtime 2026-08-20, `maxInflightPerModel: 6`
against 3 served slots, `queueTimeoutMs: 600000` against the current 7,200,000. The router
admitted 6, the overflow queued invisibly inside llama-server where `queueWaitMs` is not
measured, and the 600 s relay guard — whose comment claimed it "has never fired on healthy
work" — 502'd a healthy queued lens twice at upstreamMs 600,001 and 600,003. The lens then
succeeded in 353 s. The constant-level test passed the whole time, because it pins the module
constants and the router loads the file.

The fix: `start_services` regenerates the config and READS THE FILE BACK before the
supervisor is handed the path, refusing the run when the admission block on disk disagrees
with the served slot count; and `queueTimeoutMs` moves into `ROUTER_MACHINE_KEYS` — it is
derived from a constant that carries an invariant against the sub-session watchdog, and the
"hand edit" theory is what let a dead generation's value re-time every queued request. Effect,
stated honestly: ~24 s of aborted prefill and two phantom 502s per affected run, zero
wall-clock or throughput change. What it buys is that a stale file on disk can no longer
silently govern an experiment — the class this campaign has now paid for three times.

## D53 — the live console reported a prior run's decode as this run's total

`conductor/tools/observe.ts` handed `joinLedger` the ENTIRE unwindowed
`.data/router/metrics.jsonl` — thousands of rows across every run the machine has ever
served — and keyed the join on `group`, which is the work-root path and therefore
byte-identical across every run of the same task. Each role's bucket was the union of
every historical run and the head truncation served the OLDEST rows, so the console
reported the epoch-22 conductor arm at **37,053** completion tokens against a windowed
truth of **82,865**. Turn #2 rendered `10700/701` — a row stamped the previous day —
where the run's own row is `10700/305`.

The 45,812-token "reasoning gap" in the campaign brief was 82,865 − 37,053: arithmetic
on a broken counter, not a measurement. There was never an accounting gap. Windowed and
summed directly, the per-role figures reconcile to llama-server's own `predicted_n` to
the token: orchestrator 7,089 · mechanical 455 · skeptic 1,315 · planner 34,178 ·
reviewer 23,939 · testWriter 15,889, and 16,685 + 21,833 + 82,865 = 121,383, which is
llama-server's total for the window.

The fix windows the ledger by the run's OWN journal span — `completedAt` between the
first journal record and the last plus a 60-second grace. The grace is not slack: c828's
final ledger row (testWriter, 511 completion tokens) completed 139 ms AFTER the journal's
last record, because a request in flight when the last record lands finishes after it,
and a strict window loses exactly those tokens. `ledgerStartLine` was rejected as the key
— it is a driver-trace field written only when a cell SCORES, so it does not exist during
the live run the console is for.

The `group` filter is now a secondary guard rather than the key: 12 of the 46 windowed
rows carry `group=null` — including ALL EIGHT reviewer rows, because the router records
no group for a session with neither a worktree nor an item id — so filtering on it drops
60% of the conductor decode. Totals are a direct sum over the windowed rows rather than a
sum over joined turns, so an unjoinable turn cannot silently subtract; a null-token row
renders as `unknown`, never as a zero that reads as free. The console prints per-role
sums, which is the live cost signal a watcher actually reads.

Three predicted effects were checked and DROPPED as causally impossible from this site:
`mismatches 10 → 0` (mismatch is recommended-vs-actual, computed before the join and
reading no ledger field — the 10 marks are real doctrine-adherence signal), `COMPACTION
80m06s → 60m00s` (also computed before the join), and `turns 29 → 46` (the console already
renders 46; the 29 is `run_and_watch`'s own display trim).

Separately, `scripts/epoch_review.py`'s cross-epoch trend table now keys on `startedIso`.
A results directory holding a cell JSON is `conductor_bench`'s resume ledger, so a later
epoch can carry an earlier epoch's cell file byte for byte: the grid2048 baseline and
doctrine cells appear in four step directories with ONE `startedIso` between them, and
`INDEX.md` rendered them as four independent PASS rows. A carried cell now renders as
`=<the epoch that measured it>`.

## D54 — a phase boundary re-prefilled the whole conversation, and it is now measured

Epoch 22's orchestrator went cold on exactly three turns — 206.7 s, 238.9 s and 288.6 s of
prefill for 104, 114 and 63 decoded tokens — and each one matches an FSM transition
(DECOMPOSED 07:07:43, PLANNED 07:35:44, PLAN_REVIEWED 08:37:04). Every other orchestrator
turn was warm at `cache_n` = previous total minus one. The cause: `buildSystemAppend`
pushed the live state block LAST into `output.system`, and that block's `Run state:` and
`Next action:` lines change at every phase boundary. The system array IS the KV-cache
prefix of the request.

MEASURED HERE, not argued. A probe through the router at the shape a real orchestrator
turn has — a stable system prefix, the volatile block, then ~31k tokens of conversation
history — driven across three phase states:

| | re-prefilled tokens | prefill |
|---|---:|---:|
| volatile block in the SYSTEM prefix | 31,042 · 31,043 | 187.1 s · 187.4 s |
| byte-stable prefix, state at the USER tail | 61 · 62 | 0.6 s · 0.6 s |

`cache_n` is **0** in the first row — a total loss, exactly the c828 signature — and
30,997 of 31,058 in the second. A 99.8% cut in re-prefilled tokens per phase boundary.

A FIRST probe measured the same change at only 516 tokens and would have reported the
effect as trivial. It was wrong because it carried no conversation history: with nothing
after the divergence point the invalidated suffix is just the block itself. What makes the
loss total in a real run is that the history sits AFTER the system prompt, so a byte
changed in the prefix invalidates every turn accumulated since. The probe shape is the
finding as much as the number is.

The fix keeps the doctrine packs in the system append, where they are byte-stable for the
life of a session, and moves ONLY the volatile fields to the request tail — delivered by
`tool.execute.after`, which wire-notes 20.5 measured as the one channel that reaches the
model at the tail. It rides EVERY tool result, not once per session like the §3.8 banner.
The system entry that remains is a stable anchor naming the session's assigned item (written
once at dispatch) and telling the model to trust only the newest tail block; the tail opens
with `Conductor live state (supersedes every earlier state block)`, because moving it into
remembered history means stale copies accumulate by design.

`live-inject.test.ts` pins both halves against a REAL opencode and a stub provider: no
system message may carry a `Run state:` or `Next action:` line, and every tool result must
carry the tail with the gate's own recommendation in it.

THE COST, stated rather than buried: the block used to be re-stated in the system prompt
and left no residue, and it now accumulates — one copy per tool result, permanently, in
remembered history. At ~100 tokens a copy and 46 turns that is ~4,600 tokens of a 131,072
window, about 3.5%, bought for 187 seconds of prefill per phase boundary. The accumulation
is also why the supersedes line is load-bearing rather than decorative: a model reading an
old copy would navigate from a position the run has left, and the §6.4 doctrine sentence
"re-stated every request, never remembered" is no longer literally true of the delivery
mechanism — only of the derivation.

## D55 — the reasoning budget is a tail bound, and the 48% saving it was sold on is refuted

93.1% of epoch 22's conductor decode was reasoning, and the synthesis proposed a flat
3,072-token per-turn cap worth a 48.3% cut. Fitting the budgets against the run's OWN
per-turn distribution refutes that figure. Measured from the cell's message store, splitting
each assistant message's output tokens across its parts by character share (n turns, median,
p95 reasoning tokens):

| role | n | median | p95 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| mechanical | 2 | 180 | 260 |
| orchestrator | 14 | 157 | 362 |
| skeptic | 4 | 292 | 469 |
| testWriter | 5 | 177 | 3,272 |
| reviewer | 4 | 4,731 | 12,106 |
| planner | 4 | 6,454 | 17,187 |

A 3,072 cap clips 9 of 43 messages — and the messages it clips are the planner's and the
reviewer's, whose median healthy turns are 6,454 and 4,731 tokens of reasoning and which
COMPLETED. Fitting every budget above its role's p95 on that reasoning saves **1.2%** of
completed-turn decode, which is where this entry first landed.

THAT 1.2% IS ITSELF WRONG, and the error is instructive: it is computed over messages with
REPORTED output tokens, and a message that never finished has none. The runaways — the
expensive case, the whole reason for a bound — fall out of their own denominator.

The paired replay settles it against the model rather than against the store. The four c828
plan-review briefs were rebuilt through the real `lensPrompt` over that run's own `plan.md`
and `queue.json`, and replayed ONE AT A TIME at −1 and at 3,072:

| lens | −1 | 3,072 |
|---|---|---|
| correctness | 13,172 tokens, 2 findings | 3,345, 1 finding |
| completeness | 6,719, **0 findings** (`{"findings":[]}`) | 3,325, 1 finding |
| decomposition | 6,341, 1 finding | 2,643, 1 finding |
| minimality | **16,384 — the output cap — and NO reply at all** | 2,708, valid, 0 findings |
| **sum** | **42,616** | **12,021 (−71.8%)** |

Three findings either way, for 28% of the tokens. No reply that validated at −1 stopped
validating. The `forced_message` assertion holds on the two lenses the bound actually bit,
so this is a budget that armed rather than a null result — the distinction the measurement
was designed to make.

The unbudgeted arm's largest single line item is `minimality` spending its ENTIRE
16,384-token output allowance in the thinking channel and returning zero characters: 38% of
that arm's decode bought nothing. Under the bound the same lens answers in 2,708 tokens.
That is the D48 output-cap signature ("output-cap hits at exactly 16,384") reappearing in
the reviewer role, and it is what the 71.8% is mostly made of — not thrift on healthy turns.

So the reviewer ships at **3,072, below its own measured p95**, on this evidence and not on
the conservative rule. Every other budgeted role keeps a bound above its p95, because no
replay has been run for them and the conservative bound is the only honest one without one.

The mechanism is per-REQUEST and conductor-only: `reasoning_budget_tokens` and
`reasoning_budget_message` are set on the `chat.params` hook's `output.options`, which
`live-inject.test.ts` now verifies arrive as TOP-LEVEL fields of a real provider request
body. llama-server reads both off the request with precedence over its server-wide value.
The server-wide `--reasoning-budget` flag stays REFUTED and untouched: one llama-server
serves all three arms, so a server-wide clamp helps the conductor arm 6-19× more than the
flat arms and voids every previously scored cell.

The PLANNER is deliberately left unbudgeted, as an ESCALATION rather than an omission. It
is 88.9% reasoning and 41% of the arm's decode — the largest single prize on the list — but
it is the one role where deliberation may be load-bearing, and no cost metric in this
repository can see a cheaper plan that is worse. That trade needs a scored cell to judge
against.

### Two things the replay found that the criterion would not have caught

**The measuring harness read the wrong row.** The replay driver took "the last ledger row"
immediately after each response completed, and the router had not always flushed the new
row yet — so a lens could be scored with its PREDECESSOR's tokens. Caught by an identical
`predicted_n` on two consecutive lenses: `decomposition` was recorded at 6,719 where its own
row says **6,341**. The verdict is recomputed from the ledger, which is append-only in
completion order and maps 1:1 onto the lens order because the replay ran strictly one at a
time. The response-derived fields — validity, findings count, reasoning and text characters
— come from the reply body and were never affected. This is the instrument-disagreement
class the loop design already names: two instruments that should agree, and the one that
was easier to read was wrong.

**Schema validity does not separate a review from a silence.** At budget −1 — with no
budget in play at all — the `completeness` lens spent 26,306 characters of reasoning and
emitted **twenty characters** of reply: `{"findings":[]}`, zero findings. That validates
against the Findings schema, and review doctrine reads an empty review as the approval. So
the synthesis's stated criterion ("all four replies still validate") would score a lens that
reviewed nothing as a lens that passed. The verdict therefore compares findings COUNT per
lens beside validity: a budgeted lens that goes quieter than its unbudgeted twin has been
made cheaper by being made useless, which is the well-formed-empty-answer class this
campaign has already paid for twice.

It appears in BOTH arms and moves in both directions — `completeness` goes 0 → 1 under the
bound, `minimality` returns an empty review where unbudgeted it returned nothing at all, and
`correctness` goes 2 → 1. Total yield is three findings either way. So the empty review is a
standing defect of the reviewer stage, independent of the budget, and it needs its own
entry: a lens whose whole reply is `{"findings":[]}` should not be indistinguishable from a
lens that looked and found nothing. At n=1 per cell and temperature 0.3, the per-lens counts
are too small to read as a quality ranking; what they support is the narrower claim that the
bound did not silence the review, not that it improved it.

## D56 — a stall the router is structurally blind to, and the detector that sees it

Epoch 22's terminal event produced no signal any in-band guard could catch. A test-writer
session parked on a permission prompt had NO request in flight at all, so the router's
600 s per-read timeout had nothing to time out, llama-server logged no task, and the
plugin's own event stream had already gone quiet. The last ledger row and the last journal
record are the same second — 09:01:54Z — and the console's final frame is 10:20:37Z. The
signature of that whole failure class is not silence in an event stream; it is **no
completed HTTP request**, whatever the cause: a blocked `question`, a blocked `edit: "ask"`,
opencode's base `doom_loop` or `external_directory` narrowing, or any of the 24 non-question
watchdog deaths already in the wiring table.

The detector lives in the watcher (`run_and_watch.stall_alarm`, verdict in
`conductor_wiring.stall_verdict`), keyed off the newest of the ledger's last `completedAt`,
the journal's last record and the watcher's own start. The start is in that set so a ledger
whose newest row belongs to yesterday's run cannot fire the alarm before this run has made
a single request.

The threshold is **45 minutes**, sized above the measured healthy maxima rather than chosen
round: the largest healthy single generation on record is 26.9 minutes (a reviewer lens,
5,615 tokens at 3.48 tok/s) and the largest healthy gap between plugin-observable events is
30.0 minutes — twice, on lenses that then SUCCEEDED on retry. A 20-minute silence deadline
kills roughly one healthy dispatch in ten, preferentially in planner and reviewer, which
are 70% of the arm's decode.

It ABORTS NOTHING. It prints a loud console block on every poll and appends one sentinel
line per episode to the run directory; the watching session applies snapshot → kill →
record. That is the correction the refuted `no-progress-deadline` candidate needed: a
fanout-side watchdog resolves its job before the retry loop can run, so a terminal fire
would have destroyed the two lens retries that actually completed epoch 22's plan-review
wave.

REPLAYED OFFLINE against every conductor journal on disk, at a 20-second poll:

| run | span | fires |
|---|---:|---|
| step1 e83f | 41.5 min | zero |
| step2 bc31 | 34.6 min | zero |
| step3 a209 | 43.8 min | zero |
| step4 a7d8 | 52.4 min | zero |
| step5 6f26 | 48.9 min | zero |
| step6 f9ff (the 8-hour cell, 99.2% request-busy) | 478.1 min | zero |
| step7 9832 | 322.8 min | zero |
| step8 c828 (the stall) | 146.2 min | **first fire 09:47:02Z** |

Zero false positives across 1,022 minutes of healthy running including the full 8-hour
cell, and on the one real stall it fires at the first poll after the 45-minute mark past
the last completed request at 09:01:54Z — 33 minutes before the operator noticed, and 78.7
minutes before the run was killed by hand.
